video:video.video:title: 1Password Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's the polished, category-leading pick, and it's priced like it: free and cheaper managers exist, so you're paying for the UX, ecosystem and business controls, not raw functionality. For a business, that's usually worth it.

video:video.video:title: Adwisely Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest math is 10% of the ad spend Adwisely manages, with the monthly minimum as a floor rather than a fee on top: on Self-Serve you pay $49 below about $490 of spend, $500 at $5,000, and never more than $3,250 a month. It is cheap at low spend, but at higher budgets it's a real percentage cut of your marketing dollars until the cap, so calculate the effective cost at your actual spend, not the $49 sticker. It's built for e-commerce retargeting/prospecting on Meta and Google specifically, so it's not a general campaign manager. For stores that want largely hands-off retargeting, it removes real work.

video:video.video:title: AfterSell Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Post-purchase upsells only move the needle with steady order volume and a sensible complementary-offer strategy: bolt it onto a store with little traffic and there's nothing to upsell. The no-rev-share model is a genuine plus over percentage-based rivals.

video:video.video:title: AhaSlides Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: AhaSlides runs regional pricing: the number on the pricing page depends on where you browse from, so any review quoting one price (including ours) may not match yours. The advertised savings assume annual commitment, and the free tier's five-quiz-slide cap nudges real quiz use toward paid.

video:video.video:title: Airwallex Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest headline here is that the FX markup is published at all: 0.5% and 1% above interbank is a real number, and most competitors will not print one. What the page does not settle is everything around it. The Grow plan's platform fee 'varies with team size' with no table, so the $12 a user is not the whole subscription -- though their table does say the first ten Spend users are free, which is the part the headline rate hides in your favour. Chargeback and dispute fees are not priced anywhere, only mentioned as a feature. And the page's own disclaimer says per-transaction fees apply to certain transactions with the detail in a separate fee schedule. So: use the published FX rate to compare against your bank, then ask for the fee schedule and the platform fee before you move money. It also helps to know whose balance sheet holds what. The US page names Airwallex US, LLC as a licensed money transmitter (NMLS #1928093) that works with Lead Bank and Evolve Bank & Trust, both Member FDIC, for some US customers; the card is issued by Community Federal Savings Bank; and Yield is a brokerage product of Airwallex Capital US LLC that invests in AAA-rated money market funds, such as those from JP Morgan Asset Management. Support differs by plan too: the plan cards put a dedicated account manager and onboarding support on Accelerate only.

video:video.video:title: Algomo Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The credit model is clear on paper with one opaque step: whether a conversation was 'useful', and so billed at five credits, is decided by a language model after it closes. Algomo shows the verdict and lets you contest it, but the bill rests on a classifier you do not control. The other edges are deliberate. You cannot buy top-ups, so a traffic spike ends with the agent switched off rather than with an overage invoice; nothing is prorated when you change rungs; and cancelling drops the account to Free, where any balance above 140 credits is trimmed. On security, Algomo states that it has not completed a SOC 2 audit, and conversations go to OpenAI by default, with Anthropic, Google and Mistral models reached through OpenRouter only if you select one.

video:video.video:title: Alidrop Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Alidrop's pitch includes faster-shipping (including US/EU) suppliers, but the core dropshipping economics still apply: you pay the subscription plus wholesale product cost, and margins live or die on product selection and ad efficiency, not the tool. The low Starter product cap nudges serious stores up to Pro quickly, and as with any dropshipping automation, the platform reduces but doesn't remove supplier-quality and shipping-time risk. Sample before you scale.

video:video.video:title: Alli AI Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The entry is $299 a month paid monthly, agency-grade automation priced accordingly, and every tier meters on FOUR axes at once (sites, seats, keywords, pages). Growth on any axis costs extra, though at least the rates are published: from $39 per extra site, $24.99 per 100 extra keywords and $14.99 per 250 extra pages on monthly Business. And the category caveat an honest review owes you: bulk automated on-page edits are powerful, but changes at scale deserve human review: unchecked automated SEO is how sites break. One more thing the pricing page does not answer, and it matters at $299 a month: their own FAQ says your site, CMS and code stay untouched, so where changes are delivered through that snippet they last exactly as long as the subscription does. Price this as renting an improvement, not buying one, and ask them directly what happens to applied changes after you cancel before you commit a year.

video:video.video:title: Alohi Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest catch is that Alohi is a suite of separate products: Fax.Plus, Sign.Plus, Scan.Plus: each with its own subscription, so "one ecosystem" can mean several line items if you want e-signatures and faxing and scanning. Page and member limits on the lower tiers are modest, and HIPAA/BAA sits only on the top tier. For a single job (say online faxing), it's clean and cheap; for the full workflow, add up the parts.

video:video.video:title: Alvys Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two honest boundaries. Implementation runs to weeks, the vendor's own pricing FAQ says most operations are live in under two to four weeks, and real-time support is the top tier's: self-serve on Foundations, chat and email on Growth, phone and a dedicated success manager only on Scale. And it's built specifically for truck-based FTL operations: if you're a pure-play (non-asset) broker, run LTL with multiple customers per load, or need rail/air/ocean tracking, this isn't your TMS: Alvys itself is refreshingly explicit about that. The fit is narrow and deep, not broad.

video:video.video:title: Amplitude Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Unlimited seats is unusual and worth the credit: you are not taxed for letting the whole team look. The cost lands on events instead, and events are the thing you control least: an instrumentation change or a growth spurt moves your bill without anyone choosing to upgrade. What the plan cards do not print, the page's own bill estimator does, and we read the whole Plus ladder there on 17 September and again, unchanged, on 4 October 2026. What it shows is how little volume buys you: the marginal million events costs $94 a month at the bottom of the ladder and still $86.25 at the 70-million ceiling where Plus stops, and above that ceiling nothing is published. And 'expanded packages are priced as a percentage of your platform plan' means the add-ons scale with your bill rather than with your usage of them: the more events you send, the more the extras cost, whether or not you use them more. Get the per-event rate in writing before you instrument.

video:video.video:title: Aspire Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's a fintech account (strongest in Southeast Asia), not a full bank: great for keeping fixed costs near zero on mostly-domestic activity, but confirm it supports your country and currencies before you build your finances around it.

video:video.video:title: Audionotes Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Free voice notes stop at one minute each, so it is a trial for anything longer than a quick thought. The support page says paid subscriptions are not refunded. The app records from the device microphone, not from the speakers, and the terms mention Personal and Ultra plans that the pricing page does not show.

video:video.video:title: Audiorista Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The $29 Demo tier cannot actually publish to the App Store or Google Play: real branded apps start at $240 a month. The Business tier adds a per-active-user fee from $0.80 on top of $400 per app, so growth literally raises the bill, and Apple and Google's own store commissions still apply to in-app sales on top of everything. The Lite plan's 200 included monthly active users is also a ceiling with no published price above it; the pricing page publishes the $0.80 starting rate per monthly active listener only for Business and Enterprise.

video:video.video:title: BabyLoveGrowth Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest concern here isn't the price: it's the model, and the guarantee that is supposed to cover you if the model fails. Auto-publishing 30 to 120 AI articles a month while swapping backlinks with 4,000 other member sites is exactly the scaled-content-and-reciprocal-links pattern Google's spam policies are written to catch, and the vendor's own FAQ describes the exchange in those terms: your site places links for others as theirs place links for you. It can lift metrics short-term; on a brand you're building for years, it's a real durability risk. The 90-day money-back guarantee used to offset some of that, and we can no longer say it does: the plan cards promise it, and the FAQ on the same page says no refunds are given after the three-day trial ends. Ask for those terms in writing before you pay for a year.

video:video.video:title: Bitdefender Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The price you see is already discounted: the configurator applies 30% off list by default on all three GravityZone tiers, so compare on the discounted figure and ask what applies at renewal rather than assuming the same 30% comes back. Add-ons are billed separately too: web access and device control, network attack defense and risk management, and setup each carry their own line. Protection scores are consistently strong, so the real trade-off is cost, not efficacy.

video:video.video:title: Blocky Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
Read the plan text before you read the badge. The App Store header says a free plan is available; that free plan is Development Stores, for development and partner stores only, and it starts charging the moment the store goes live. All three paid tiers then carry the line 'all stores except for Shopify Plus stores', so if you are on Plus this app is not sold to you. Check that with the developer before you plan around it.
A blocker is a blunt instrument, and the review distribution shows it: 355 reviews read on 5 October 2026, 89% of them at the top rating and 5% at the bottom: eighteen one-star reviews, three of them added between late August and mid-September. Rules that stop fraud also stop customers. A blocked country catches the expat who wanted to buy; a VPN rule catches the privacy-minded shopper. The tuning is yours to do, continuously, using visitor analytics that only the Pro tier includes.
And it prevents rather than recovers. Nothing here disputes a chargeback that has already landed or claws back an order that already shipped. For that you need a separate dispute tool, which is a second subscription on top of this one.

video:video.video:title: Boulevard Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two things about this price list. It is per location, so the arithmetic for a second salon is not a volume discount, it is double, and the add-ons are per location too, which compounds it. And the prices you see are annual-billing rates: the page opens on its Annually tab and the toggle puts monthly billing about 11% higher ($159 against $143 on Essentials, read 4 October 2026), so the sticker is the cheapest version of the number. Two of the three tiers still show that sticker struck through against a higher 'normally' figure, footnoted on 17 September 2026 as a limited-time offer for new customers only, and relabelled 'fall pricing' by 4 October on the same terms; treat the higher number as the list price a renewal may return to. Essentials shows what that looks like when the music stops: on 18 August it was $140 against a struck-through $176, and a month later the discount and the comparison are both gone and it reads $143. The third thing is not a price at all: you cannot buy this without booking a demo. That is a signal about how the deal is done, and it means the published numbers are a starting point rather than a checkout.

video:video.video:title: Bread & Butter Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two meters to watch: it prices per WEBSITE (multi-site setups multiply the $49) and the AI features run on compute-credit blocks that stack as usage grows. On privacy, refined twice in open dialogue with the vendor (16 Jul 2026, verified against their docs). The anonymous journey IS tracked from the first visit, server-side via their site plugin. So ad-blockers and Safari’s ITP don’t strip it the way they kill client-side scripts: the vendor estimates 30-50% of high-value traffic is lost to client-side blocking. What stays dormant until someone submits an email is identity resolution: the ‘hand-raise’ that connects the captured history to a verified person. You still owe normal GDPR care on enriched data, and the real trade-off is simply this: no IP-based guessing at which company an anonymous visitor works for.

video:video.video:title: Breezy HR Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The jump from free (one position) to the first paid tier is steep if you only hire occasionally: the free plan is usable, so live in it until you're filling several roles at once.

video:video.video:title: Brevo Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Charging by sends looks cheaper for a big list you email rarely, but the send tiers cap stored contacts too: 5,000 sends a month stores only 500 contacts, and a 20,000-contact list needs the 20,000-send tier whatever you send. Model both numbers first, and the free daily cap and add-on fees on top.

video:video.video:title: Bright Data Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: This is enterprise-grade web data infrastructure at enterprise-grade prices: the per-GB meter looks small until you multiply by real scraping volume, and the committed tiers only pay off if your usage is steady. The bigger honest note is compliance: Bright Data is strict about KYC and use-cases (a feature, not a bug), and whatever you collect still has to respect the target sites' terms and applicable law. Budget legal thought alongside the gigabytes.

video:video.video:title: Brizy Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Personal covers one website and each extra site costs $17 a month. E-commerce sites are priced separately under Brizy Shops, and the WordPress plugin has its own pricing, so the Cloud prices are not the whole picture. Our own test on 5 November 2026 stayed on the free Cloud trial, where the AI request was blocked; paid plans were not part of it. Brizy's terms (last updated 7 October 2026) narrow the money-back promise on the pricing page: the 30-day refund covers new monthly or yearly subscriptions only, not renewals, lifetime licences, add-ons or anything bought outside brizy.io, and auto-renewal has to be switched off at least 24 hours before the renewal date. The terms are governed by the laws of the United Kingdom, with an arbitration clause you can opt out of by email within 30 days.

video:video.video:title: BrowserAct Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The free tier is the catch: its card reads 200 signup credits where it read 1,500 on 2 September, about 66 workflow steps at 3 credits a step, while the vendor's own llms.txt still advertises 2,000. And the 'as low as' step rate does not come from these tiers: llms.txt puts a step at about $0.0019, but at Advanced a credit works out to about $0.00096, so a 3-credit step is roughly $0.0029 -- the lower number must belong to a credit pack whose price the page does not show. In our hands-on run of 4 September (historical test data, priced at the meters of that day) the meter was honest at account level (1,500 to 1,174 credits over one build and two runs, reconciling exactly with the history list), but the same Bot cost 21 credits on one run and 27 on the next for identical output, and the task panel briefly reported 0 credits for a run the list priced at 21.

video:video.video:title: BuddyPunch Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: That flat $19 base fee makes it pricey for very small teams: at three or four users the base fee dominates the bill, so it's better value once you're past a handful of employees. Two further limits come from Buddy Punch's own documentation. The free administrator seat cannot clock its own time, so a working owner pays for a second login. And outbound webhooks do not yet cover punches or time cards, so a payroll or HR system that needs live punch events has to poll the API instead.

video:video.video:title: Buzz.ai Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two meters run at once: seats AND credits: the seat price includes a credit allowance (500 a month on Core, 5,000 on AI Employee, read 7 November 2026), and real outbound volume means credit packages on top, so budget past the sticker. Watch the moving numbers too: the page changed three times since August: a $75 teaser, then $79 a seat on Core; $795 with a promised rise to $1,000, then $695, and since November no published AI Employee price at all, with a two-seat minimum, and Enterprise carries a $2,500 setup fee, so decide on the total for the plan you are actually offered, not the sticker. And the honest fundamental for any AI-SDR: it only books meetings as good as your list and offer, so keep a human reviewing what goes out in your name.

video:video.video:title: Castmagic Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The prices on the page are the annual prices. The toggle sits on “Annually — Save 30% Annually” by default, so $19, $48 and $139 are what you pay when you commit for a year. The month-to-month figures are readable in the page source and they are $29, $69 and $199, so the gap is real and on the entry tier it is wider than advertised: Hobby is about 34% cheaper annually, not 30%.
The hours are the part to pin down before you subscribe. The comparison table labels them “transcribed hours (library total)”, and the FAQ describes “a growing library of transcribed hours ... that you build up over time”. That wording fits a monthly allowance and a lifetime ceiling equally well, and the difference between the two is enormous. 30 hours every month at $19 is a bargain for a weekly podcast. 30 hours in total is about seven episodes, and then you are buying top-ups. Ask before you pay, and ask what happens to the hours when you downgrade.
And the social proof does not agree with itself: now in three directions. The pricing page says “75k+ Creators Served” and “75,000+ Creators & Businesses”; the homepage hero says “Loved by 100K+ podcasters and creators”; and the site's own llms.txt claims “200,000+ creators — including 100,000+ podcasters and 75,000+ creators and teams”. Three numbers, one site, and they cannot all be current. It is a small thing, and the kind of small thing that tells you which numbers on a marketing site have been checked recently. Treat the totals, the 10M minutes and the named logos as marketing, and judge the product on the trial.

video:video.video:title: ChatGPT AI Product Description Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
First, the name is not a name. 'ChatGPT AI Product Description' describes a category, the app's own listing copy now calls itself Descrii AI Product Descriptions, and Shopify shows a different app by a different developer under a nearly identical name on the same page. Check the developer is Profitonium before you install.
Second, the credit is undefined and it is the only thing you are buying. Four tiers, one variable, no definition, and the '$1 per 100 descriptions' line repeated on all three paid plans is not the rate on two of them. Worse, the plan price may not be the whole bill: the listing carries Shopify's usage-based-charges line, and a merchant of twelve months, in a review edited 30 July 2026, itemised charges of $586.79, $487.49, $282.69 and $483.16 on top of a stated $149 a year plus $49 a month, marked 'billing cycle ended' and 'fee threshold reached'. That is one public account and the developer has not answered it on the listing, but nothing on the page lets you rule it out either.
Third, and the one that costs real money: this app edits your live store. Its permissions cover product descriptions and titles, Online Store pages and theme, files, locales, Shopify Markets settings, translations and navigation, and nothing on the listing describes versioning, a preview queue or a rollback. On 15 September 2026 a merchant of five months reported that it changed titles to products the store does not carry; the developer replied the next day that he had paused automatic generation for that store and was adding safeguards. The 529 ratings are strong, 504 five stars, but three are one star and they are the ones that describe undoing. Export your product CSV before the first bulk run. That is your rollback.

video:video.video:title: Clonable Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's a continuous subscription, not a one-time translation: you pay every month to keep the translated clone synced with your site. It's also machine translation under the hood, so quality varies by language pair; have a native speaker spot-check high-stakes pages. Worth knowing before you compare tiers: the pricing page opens on its annual setting, so the figure you see first is not what a monthly subscription costs.

video:video.video:title: Clutch Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's free to submit a brief, but be clear on what it is: a lead-generation marketplace, not a neutral directory. Your brief goes straight to agencies who will reach out to pitch you, and providers pay to be visible and matched. It's a fast way to shortlist vetted agencies; just expect the outreach that comes with it.

video:video.video:title: Connecteam Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The free-for-10 plan is one of the most generous in the category, but the three-hub structure means costs can stack if you need all of them: price the specific hubs you'll actually use, not the full bundle. Read two terms before paying: a monthly plan can be cancelled at any time but prepaid amounts are not refunded, and an annual plan is refundable pro rata only within its first 30 days. Every price is in US dollars, with no other currency offered.

video:video.video:title: Consensus Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It searches peer-reviewed literature, which is its strength and its boundary: it can tell you what published studies found, not whether those studies are good. Study quality, sample sizes and conflicting results still need your judgment, and the AI summary layer can smooth over genuine scientific disagreement. Treat it as a dramatically faster literature scan, not an oracle; click through to the papers that matter. Consensus's own developer notes (read 21 October 2026) add three limits worth knowing before you pay. The corpus is English-first: non-English papers are indexed where metadata exists, but ranking and summaries are tuned for English. It is not a news feed: papers published in the last few weeks may not be indexed yet. And the Consensus Meter is described as a heuristic, not a formal meta-analysis.

video:video.video:title: Contabo Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The advertised prices are for a 24-month term, and that term is prepaid: the Cloud VPS 12 configurator asked €480.00 upfront. Month-to-month costs about 25% more. Backups (€6.70 a month on that size), Windows Server, cPanel and Plesk are paid add-ons, and the servers are unmanaged. Traffic is unlimited only under a fair-use policy that lets Contabo throttle heavy users. Prices on the page exclude VAT. We have not used Contabo ourselves. The refund routes are narrow. The 14-day revocation is for private accounts only: business accounts and domains are excluded, and you must confirm that all data on the server will be lost. After an automatic renewal, a refund is possible if you contact support within 72 hours, except for customers in Germany. Outside those windows, cancelling only stops the next billing cycle. Contabo supports the server, the network and the initial setup of 1-click add-ons; maintaining, upgrading and troubleshooting the software on it is your job.

video:video.video:title: Convert Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The meter is tested users, and it keeps running: blow past your monthly allowance and overuse blocks land at $399-699 unless you hard-cap them, and every extra custom domain is $1,000 a year. The friendly $299 headline assumes annual prepay; month-to-month is $399. One thing people misprice, and it is not the test itself: everyone expects an experiment to end when the subscription does. The trap is the winner. Convert describes itself as a client-side tool where “adding just one snippet of code on your site will then do all of the magic”. So a winning variant you leave running in the visual editor is not a change to your site: it is a rendering by their script. Ship the winner into your own code, or you are paying rent on a result you already bought.

video:video.video:title: Create Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The middle package is a shop with most of the shop tools missing. Professional's ecommerce column on the pricing page has a 250-product limit and discount codes, and then a dash on nine lines: abandoned basket recovery, Instagram and Facebook Shopping, selling digital products, Google Shopping, Klarna, PayPal pay-later, Pinterest Shopping, product customisation and Royal Mail Click & Drop. If you sell downloads, want basket-recovery emails or want your products in Google Shopping, the real price is Business at €39.99 a month, twice Professional.
The prices are shown without VAT. The page says VAT is added at the prevailing rate for your country, so a seller who cannot reclaim it pays more than the headline: at 20%, Business is €47.99 a month. The page also showed us euros from the Netherlands; check which currency your account will be billed in before you compare it with a dollar-priced builder.
Team editing is thin below the tailored tier. Professional allows one website administrator and Business three; only Tailored, from €79.99, mentions permissions for unlimited staff. A shop with a part-time helper on Professional means sharing one login.
Two things the pricing page does not tell you: how long the free trial lasts, and what card payments cost. It lists no transaction fee of Create's own, but the card fees belong to the payment provider you connect, such as Stripe, PayPal, WorldPay or Opayo. The many customer quotes on the package pages are Create's own selection. We have not used Create.
The terms of Create Internet Limited (company 03821624, registered in England and Wales) add four things to know before you sign up. The trial is given at Create's discretion and stops when it ends; you then get an email and have 90 days to subscribe, after which all content in the account is deleted. Cancelling is not a button: the terms ask you to email your Customer Account Manager, the account closes the day before the next payment, and deleting your website does not c

video:video.video:title: CrossLoop Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The money-back guarantee covers only your first purchase, and films are deleted after 30 days, so anything you do not download is gone. The pages we read do not describe editing or revisions: the film is made from what your page says, so a thin page gives a thin film. CrossLoop is run by one named person, Harsha Vardhan, according to the terms, which is worth knowing if you plan to rely on it for a long time.

video:video.video:title: CrowdStrike Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two numbers decide whether this is for you, and neither is the headline. The first is the 100-device ceiling on Falcon Go: it is not a soft limit you grow through, it is the point where you change product. The second is the annual rate, which is worth doing the division on: $59.99 a year against $7.99 a month is $95.88, so annual saves 37%, one of the larger annual discounts in security software. Beyond that, be honest with yourself about which tier you are comparing: Go is antivirus with a good agent, and the endpoint detection and response that CrowdStrike is famous for starts at Pro. Comparing Go against a full EDR product from a competitor is comparing the wrong things.

video:video.video:title: DigitalOcean Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The $4 Droplet is real, but it is the smallest machine, 512 MiB of memory, and it is only the server. Backups cost 20% (weekly) or 30% (daily) of the Droplet price on top, a managed database starts at $15 a month and a load balancer at $12, so a small production app is several line items rather than one: a 2 GiB Droplet at $12 with daily backups ($3.60) and the smallest managed database ($15) comes to $30.60 a month before any bandwidth overage. Billing is per second and in arrears, which is fair, but the bill arrives after the month you used: set a billing alert on day one.
Three operational limits catch people moving a small project from shared hosting. SMTP ports 25, 465 and 587 are blocked on all Droplets, so a self-hosted mail server, or a plugin that sends mail straight from the server, will not work; DigitalOcean points you to a delivery service such as SendGrid. A powered-off Droplet keeps billing until you destroy it. And late payment has no published clock: a past-due account cannot create resources, a suspended one has its resources powered down, and after that resources may be permanently deleted, with DigitalOcean saying it does not publish fixed timelines for these stages. After paying, you switch Droplets back on yourself. The billing FAQ answers the refund question in one line: DigitalOcean does not offer refunds.

video:video.video:title: Dynasort Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Sorting driven by 60+ blended signals is powerful and opaque in the same breath: a recipe that ranks by margin, velocity and stock at once will sometimes bury a product you wanted seen, and there is real trial and error in getting the recipes to match how you actually merchandise. The jump from free to paid is steep at $99 a month, and it buys capacity rather than capability: search, recommendations and post-purchase are already in the free Demo, and Basic multiplies collections, recipes and serves (100,000 a month against 10,000). Above that the listing contradicts itself: the $249 card says 'Everything in Pro, plus' and the $499 card 'Everything in Basic, plus' — so which tier carries A/B testing and the connector API is not something the page settles. And the evidence base is thin: 4.6 from 15 reviews, with fourteen fives and a single one-star and nothing in between. It is Shopify-only, so it is not an option if any part of your catalogue lives elsewhere.

video:video.video:title: EasyDMARC Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: You are buying domains and history, not features, and no longer seats, since every tier now lists unlimited users. Plus covers two domains. Subdomains do not count toward that, the page says they are detected automatically, but a company with a main domain, a second brand and a legacy domain it forgot about is already over. The history window is the part that bites later: three months on Plus means that when you are investigating a spoofing campaign that started in the spring, the reports are gone. And watch the volume ceiling. Read on 4 October 2026, the page's own tooltip says that once you pass your monthly quota, additional reports are not processed until the next billing cycle. There is no overage charge, just a gap in the data, and it opens precisely when a spoofing run inflates your report volume. Size the plan on your busiest month, not your average.

video:video.video:title: ElevateForward Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's a strategy-to-execution layer, not a task app or a dashboard, so the value only lands if leadership actually adopts the framework. 'Operational alignment platform' is also a fuzzy and crowded label, so press them on the concrete deliverables (the diagnostics, KPI blueprints and execution plans) before committing. Read the legal page before you submit confidential numbers. Its privacy section says report-related data is retained for internal reference and refinement unless you ask for deletion, the terms provide the application 'as-is' with no uptime guarantee, liability is capped at what you paid (for the service over the prior twelve months, or for the specific credits or reports behind a claim), and disputes go to the courts of Travis County, Texas.

video:video.video:title: ElevenLabs Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Credits are the meter and retakes are the tax: you are charged per generation request, and a regeneration is only free while the content and settings are unchanged, so real usage lands well above the calculator estimate. And read the free-tier fine print: $0 gets you 10k credits to play with, but no commercial license: anything you publish commercially needs at least the $6 Starter. Voice realism leads the market; niche names and jargon can still need manual retakes, so run your hardest paragraph through the free tier before subscribing.

video:video.video:title: EmailListVerify Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The $5 entry pack is the most expensive way to buy: $0.005 per check versus $0.00196 at the 50k tier: a 2.5x spread that rewards guessing your volume upfront. And the email finder quietly consumes 5 credits per found address (10 if you only have the domain), so a 1,000-credit pack finds at most 200 emails, not 1,000. Subscription credits also reset every month, so an unused allowance is simply lost.

video:video.video:title: Envoy Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: None of the prices on that page is a price you can budget from. Four of the five product cards are followed by 'Price excludes platform fee', and the platform page says outright that the platform is required to use Envoy products and is charged as a flat annual fee: with its own Premium and Enterprise tiers to pick first, and no number published anywhere on the site. That is the first thing to ask for. The second is how the meters stack, because they are all in different units: per location, per user, per bookable resource, per device, per delivery location. An office with forty bookable desks, six screens and one delivery point is paying on four clocks at once: $362 for the location, $200 for the desks, $250 for deliveries, and $180 for the screens rather than the $72 the card implies, because Envoy's own llms.txt sets a 15-device minimum that the pricing page never mentions. That is $992 a month before the platform fee, and before emergency notifications, which the same file bills at $2 a head across your entire employee directory rather than across the people who use them. Price the combination you actually want, not the product you came for.

video:video.video:title: Evolve Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's built for large organizations: the site claims 100+ enterprises deployed globally and 2.9M+ learners trained, with Danone among the named references, and the sales-led, quote-only motion reflects that: there is no self-serve tier to trial quietly, so smaller teams can't just kick the tires before procurement gets involved.

video:video.video:title: Fastmail Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: You're paying for what the free giants monetize differently: no ads, no profiling, real support and standards-first email (JMAP/IMAP everywhere). The honest limits: it's email/calendar/contacts, not a Workspace-style office suite, so document collaboration lives elsewhere, and migrating decades of Gmail habits (filters, integrations) takes a weekend of care. For owning your address on your own domain, it's the boring, excellent choice.

video:video.video:title: Filevine Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Nothing is priced, so everything is negotiable, which cuts both ways. In legal software the number that usually surprises people is not the per-seat rate but implementation: data migration from your existing case system, template configuration and training, quoted separately and often as a one-off in the thousands. That figure is absent here along with everything else. Ask for it as its own line, ask what the contract length is, and ask what happens to your matter data if you leave. A custom quote is fine; a custom quote you cannot compare against a rate card is what you are trying to avoid.

video:video.video:title: Flippa Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The real cost is the success fee, and it's a flat bracket rate on the whole sale price, not marginal: a mid-five-figure sale can hand over a four- to five-figure commission. Flippa is also a self-serve marketplace: more listings, but more due-diligence burden on you. Verification and quality vary, so buyers must vet hard and sellers should expect tyre-kickers. It's reach and liquidity, not a white-glove broker.

video:video.video:title: Gamma Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The credit model means heavy generation eats your monthly allowance, and outputs still need a human polish for high-stakes decks: it's a brilliant first-draft engine, not a finished-deck button. The free tier's watermark pushes you to paid quickly.

video:video.video:title: Getscreen Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: AnyDesk tends to feel faster and lower-latency, and TeamViewer carries the heavier security/compliance certifications (HIPAA, SOC 2). Getscreen's real edge is being fully browser-based, nothing to install on the other person's machine, and cheaper, especially with the lifetime deal.

video:video.video:title: Gixo Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
Two things about this pricing are worth reading twice.
The first is that seven products means seven subscriptions, and most of them are now per seat. Gixo is priced per deliverable, not per company, and one product's plan does not include the others. A team that needs decks, articles and proposals buys Lumen plus Quill plus Arc: $69 a month for one person at the entry tiers, $133 at the Starter tiers Gixo now recommends, and at least $759 a month for three people on the Professional tiers that add shared review. There is no published bundle price; the only route the page names is procurement, where private offers and multi-product bundles go through review. Ask for that before you subscribe to the second product, not after.
The second is the seat minimums (read 21 October 2026). On 4 October Quill Professional was $79 a month for three seats; it is now $79 a seat with a three-seat minimum, and every tier above the one-seat tiers on Quill, Lumen, Business, Lex and Arc works the same way. The generation allowance behind each tier is still not stated outside Folio's chapter counts, and the first step is steep on Quill: Lite at $10 is pitched at publishing now and then, the next tier is $59. Run the 14-day trial at the volume you actually expect.

video:video.video:title: Healthie Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two honest limits: it's pricier than alternatives with thin mid-tier options, and several users report slow customer service (sometimes a week or more to reply). It really only pays off at scale: solo or tiny practices get more value, more simply, elsewhere.

video:video.video:title: HiBob Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Opaque pricing and an implementation fee mean the real cost only surfaces in a sales call, and it's built for scaling mid-size companies, so it's heavy and expensive for a small team.

video:video.video:title: Imgify Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
Start with the word 'free' on the listing card, because it does not mean what it looks like. The free plan is development and partner stores only, and billing activates the moment you upgrade: a real storefront pays $2.99 from the first day, after a 7-day trial.
Then the harder question: the nearest app in the same Shopify category costs nothing. Dakaas Seasonal Effects carries the same Built for Shopify badge, lists 200+ holiday themes plus cursor effects, music and scheduling, and has 1,567 reviews at 4.9 since May 2021 against Imgify's 32 at 4.8 since January 2020. So you are not weighing $2.99 against nothing at all: you are weighing it against a free app with a public record roughly fifty times deeper.
What the money actually answers is narrow: the AI logo maker and the marquee slider for partner, payment and press logos, neither of which is on the free app's feature list. That is a real difference and it is the whole case for paying.
And treat the sales pitch as a pitch. The listing promises effects that 'boost sales' and logo rows that build 'instant trust'; no conversion data is published for either claim, by this vendor or by the free ones. Note too what the recent reviews are built from: three of the newest come from stores that had the app installed for ten minutes, about three hours and nine months respectively, so most of that 4.8 says the install went smoothly, not that the thing kept working.

video:video.video:title: Increff Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: This is enterprise omnichannel supply-chain software, and the opaque, quote-based pricing signals the target customer: retail brands with real scale, not small stores. The value (algorithmic merchandising and inventory optimization) only pays off at a catalog and volume large enough for those optimizations to move money. For a small or mid seller, it's likely more platform (and cost and implementation) than the problem warrants. For a scaling omnichannel brand, it's built for exactly that.

video:video.video:title: Insightful Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: This is employee-monitoring software, so weigh the culture cost, not just the price: the advertised $8-16 rates are per seat AND are the annual ones (month-to-month exists on select plans but is never priced), security features like insider-threat detection are a paid add-on, and monitoring tools can damage trust if rolled out without transparency.

video:video.video:title: Inworld AI Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The bill is usage on top of the plan, counted on every input character including spaces, punctuation and tags. Credits roll over only while you stay subscribed, cancelling or downgrading forfeits the rest, and payments are non-refundable. The pricing page and the docs disagree on whether zero data retention is a Growth add-on or Enterprise only, and it does not cover requests sent to third-party model providers.

video:video.video:title: Katana MRP Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: There is no public price above Free any more. Since late October 2026 the pricing page lists only Free (30 SKUs) and Advantage, a custom annual contract quoted after a scoping call, so you cannot set Katana's cost against an alternative until you have been through sales. It is capable manufacturing software and the quote bundles the modules that used to be paid add-ons; ask for the quote in writing, with the contract term and what changes if your SKU count or order volume grows.

video:video.video:title: Keap Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Cost is the big one (56% of reviewers flag it), the interface feels dated, and there's a real 2–4 week learning curve on the automation builder. Billing and cancellation complaints are common: their own terms carry a $299 early termination fee on an annual contract and require ten days' phone notice, and email design is thinner than dedicated email tools.

video:video.video:title: Keeper Security Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The per-user price is the smallest part of the bill. Read the add-ons page next to the plan page and the shape becomes clear: BreachWatch and KeeperChat are $24 per user per year each, Advanced Reporting & Alerts and Compliance Reports $12 per user per year each, endpoint privilege management $36 per endpoint per year, so a Business seat at $4.00 a month can quietly double once you add the monitoring and reporting most buyers assume is included, and Connection Manager and Secrets Manager are not even priced. Annual billing is stated on every tier, so there is no month-to-month option to test with, and Business Starter is scoped at 5–10 users. Ask for the base plan and each add-on you need as separate lines, because a bundled quote here hides which part is actually costing you.

video:video.video:title: Kinsta Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: You're paying a premium for managed speed, Google Cloud infrastructure and expert support: worth it if performance and hands-off management matter, wasteful on a low-traffic hobby site a $5 shared host would carry fine.

video:video.video:title: Kopage Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The terms say Kopage generally does not give refunds, and the trial is 7 days. The AI token allowance (10K on Solo, 100K above) comes with no published reset period or top-up price, and self-hosting a client site on Scale or Unlimited costs an extra fee that is not published. Paddle, the merchant of record, handles returns, while the refund clause is written for downloaded licences, so how a refund request on a cloud plan is treated is not spelled out. The self-hosted pricing page still carries an older FAQ (an Agency Plan with 10 sites, $5 a month per extra site and a 14-day trial per site) that does not match the current cloud plans. The Single Website plan covers one static website and is provided by Website•IM.

video:video.video:title: Lindy.ai Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Cost tracks headcount as well as output: every colleague who so much as @mentions Lindy in Slack takes a seat, and a seat you remove runs to the end of the cycle with no mid-cycle proration. Credits are sized in ranges (an everyday ask is 2-250, a big build 1,000-2,500), so a month is still an estimate. And the entry price itself was served in two versions on 8 November 2026: $29.99 for 3,000 credits or $49.99 for 5,000.

video:video.video:title: LumenCart Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
Two things decide whether this is cheap, and neither is the plan price. The first is that you buy credits, not images: highest quality costs 2 credits against 1 for standard, so the better setting halves every allowance on the page: Starter's 75 credits is 37 images a month, not 75.
The second is the one-off packs, which look like a convenient top-up and are the most expensive way to buy. On their own figures, 25 credits for $22 is about $0.88 a credit, while Starter's $9 for 75 is about $0.12 and Pro's $79 for 1,000 is about $0.08. A pack is roughly seven to eleven times the subscription rate per credit, so if you keep reaching for packs you are on the wrong plan. Monthly credits are described as refreshed each month with nothing said about rolling over, so assume an unused allowance is gone; the packs, by contrast, state a 12-month life.
The free tier is also smaller than it looks: 25 generations is a lifetime total for the store, not a monthly one, which is a single afternoon of trying looks across a catalogue. And the app is new, launched 8 August 2026 with no reviews at all on its listing at the time of writing, so there is no track record yet on image quality or on support.

video:video.video:title: MX AI Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The strongest argument against paying for this is one App Store search away. RT: Background Music Player, from RoarTheme, does the core job (upload a media file, it plays in the background) and the listing prices it at Free, full stop. It sits at 4.8 stars over 72 reviews against this app's 4.8 over 66, and it has been on the store since 5 February 2021. What the $2.99 buys over free is real but narrow: control over the player's colour, size, position, volume, loop and autoplay, sources beyond an uploaded file, and a set of AI-generated royalty-free seasonal tracks. If all you want is one MP3 looping on the homepage, you are paying for controls you will set once and never open again.
Two smaller things worth knowing before you install. The "Free plan available" badge on the listing is for development and partner stores only: on a live store there is no free tier, so read that badge as a 7-day trial. And the pitch that background music "can enhance your interaction with customers and improve conversion rate & sales" arrives with no evidence: no study, no store data, no test. Autoplay is not entirely yours to command either, because browsers block audio that starts without a user gesture, so the autoplay switch takes effect once the shopper has interacted with the page rather than on load. At $2.99 the cost of finding out whether sound helps your store is small, but find out, rather than assume.

video:video.video:title: MeetGeek Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The meter is transcription hours and Pro gives you twenty a month, which is about an hour a working day. That sounds generous until you count the meetings you would actually record: a sales rep on four calls a day passes it in the first week, and the overage is $0.50 an hour. Unlimited transcription is the real reason to be on Business at $17, so treat Pro as a plan for occasional recording rather than a cheaper version of the same thing. Worth checking before you buy: consent. A recorder that joins every meeting changes what people say in them, and that is a policy decision rather than a pricing one.

video:video.video:title: Mktg.ai Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The price is still hidden (a 404 where the pricing page should be, and no pricing item in the navigation) which for a tool that promises spend transparency is an irony worth noticing, and the FAQ makes it sharper: its own introduction says it covers what the platform costs, and then no answer in it names a figure. What the FAQ does publish is the tier names, Growth and Enterprise, and the fact that EU data residency is Enterprise-only. The ROI story is also the vendor's own: the homepage tile assumes a $5M budget and puts a 3% efficiency gain at $150K alongside $100K of reallocated spend, which is 2% of the same budget. Ask for verified case numbers at your spend level on the demo call.

video:video.video:title: Modelize Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The economics are flat: at roughly $0.19 to $0.20 an image on every tier, moving up the ladder buys resolution, custom presets and support, never a cheaper image. Read it that way and the pricing is honest; read it as a volume discount and you will overbuy. Two other things deserve a clear head. The output quality rides on Google's Gemini image models rather than on anything Modelize owns, so results and consistency can shift when Google ships a new version, and that is outside the vendor's control as much as yours. And the app is new (launched 20 April 2026, 26 reviews on 4 October 2026) so the 4.9 average is a small sample, not a track record. Finally, an on-model photo generated by AI shows a person who does not exist; check what your ad platforms and marketplaces require you to disclose before you build a catalogue on it.

video:video.video:title: Motive Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: A pricing page with a form where the prices should be. That is the finding, and it matters more in fleet than in software generally. The real cost here is not a monthly rate: it is hardware per vehicle, a contract term that is usually multi-year, and an early-termination position you will not hear about until you want out. None of that is public. Before the demo call, decide your own numbers: vehicles, contract length you will accept, and what you currently pay per truck. In a quote-only category the first number you hear is anchored to what they think you can pay, not to a rate card.

video:video.video:title: NameRobot Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: NameScore prices are shown as offers against regular prices twice as high, with no end date, and the Naming Toolbox premium price is not printed on namerobot.com. The automated trademark and availability checks are a screening, not legal clearance. NameScore is sold for commercial use and prices exclude VAT, which EU buyers without a VAT ID pay on top. We have not used NameRobot ourselves. NameRobot's terms (dated 22 July 2021, with the German version legally binding) say the checks are for research only, that NameRobot is not allowed to give legal advice and does not guarantee that a name is free of third-party rights, and that users indemnify NameRobot against claims over names they use. Premium subscriptions renew for the same period unless cancelled in writing or in the account at least two weeks before the term ends.

video:video.video:title: Nexis CRO Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
It has no track record at all. The app launched on 9 June 2026 and its App Store listing still showed a 0.0 rating from zero reviews when we read it on 14 September and again on 3 October 2026, so every claim about what the audit catches, how good the AI rewrites are and whether the citation tracking is accurate rests on the vendor's own description. That matters more than usual here, because AEO tracking is a young field: nobody has yet shown that being cited by ChatGPT or Perplexity moves revenue, and the numbers a tracker reports are hard for a merchant to check independently. The free tier is also thin: 5 AI credits and one audit a month is enough to see the interface, not to test the product.
Who is behind it is thinly documented. The listing gives the developer as Nexis Cro with an address in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, the app is English-only, and nexiscro.com links a privacy policy but no terms of service or refund policy. The privacy policy (8 June 2026) names OpenAI as the processor for AI requests, using models such as GPT-4o-mini, so product and policy text you send through AI Quick Fix leaves Shopify for OpenAI. The listing's data-access block asks for the store owner's name, email, phone number and address and for customer device and geolocation data.
The vendor's own pages also disagree on price: the llms.txt file lists Pro at $29, Growth at $59 and Agency at $149, three times the listing's $9, $21 and $44. An AEO vendor whose own machine-readable file misstates its prices is a small but telling signal about how carefully the llms.txt it deploys to your store needs checking.

video:video.video:title: NordVPN Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The €3.49 is a two-year introductory rate: Basic renews at €139.08 a year, about €11.59 a month, roughly three times what you signed up at. It's a solid, easy VPN, but a VPN is one layer of security, not a whole strategy: don't mistake it for endpoint protection.

video:video.video:title: Optery Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Core automates removals for one name and one city and state only, with no human handling exceptions; past addresses and name variations need Extended at $12.42 a month yearly. The advertised site counts assume Expanded Reach is enabled; without it Core covers 150+ sites instead of 380+. Custom removal requests on Ultimate only start after 30 days. Removals from data brokers take time and listings can reappear, which is why every paid plan rescans monthly. We have not used Optery ourselves. Personal plans are only for residents of the United States, Canada (excluding Quebec), Australia, New Zealand and South Africa (help desk, updated 25 September 2026). Optery does not remove anything from social media, forums, blogs, news sites, legal-records sites or documents posted online, and offers no dark-web scanning. Cancelling stops future billing, keeps the plan until the end of the paid term and then drops the account to Free Basic, with no pro-rated refund outside the 30-day guarantee.

video:video.video:title: Ownr Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two honest limits. It's Canada-only (provincial incorporation covers Ontario, Alberta, BC and Quebec) so it's no use outside Canada. And it's built for straightforward setups: it won't handle complex share structures, multi-investor shareholder agreements, tax planning, partnerships or non-profits. For those you still want an accountant or lawyer.

video:video.video:title: Pagecloud Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Pagecloud AI has no native blog or online store; the pricing FAQ, read on 12 October 2026, says Pagecloud AI does not currently include native blogging or ecommerce, so on Launch, Grow and Optimize you embed or link an outside service. The plans are separated by AI usage that the page gives only as multipliers with no numbers, and AI is free 'for typical use' during a beta, so what you will pay for AI once the beta ends is not on the page. Launch includes no team members. The older Pagecloud Classic builder is kept for existing customers only (llms.txt, read 25 October 2026), so this review covers only the Pagecloud AI plans. The terms renew a subscription automatically unless notice is given at least ten days before it ends and say payments are non-refundable; after a suspension or termination Pagecloud says it will try to help you retrieve data within 10 days. There is no import of an existing site yet.

video:video.video:title: Papaya Global Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Every headline price is a 'starting from' that dead-ends at 'book a demo'. And multiple reviewers report the real bill runs bigger than the sticker: 30-50% over quote, with setup, FX and filing fees surfacing after signing (reviewer reports, not universal terms). The documented contract is typically a two-year agreement with a rolling 90-day termination clause, so read the term and exit clauses closely before signing. The deeper structural knock is where the work happens. Outside the countries where Papaya owns entities, it delivers EOR through in-country partners; a third-party estimate puts the owned count near 40, and Papaya does not disclose which are owned versus partner. So at 15+ countries you're often one escalation removed from whoever actually runs your payroll. Clients report a recurring set of problems: invoicing errors, data that doesn't sync between Papaya and the partner, and missed or late payroll runs. Support decays from a named account manager into a rotating ticket queue with no live channel.

video:video.video:title: Passpack Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The honest trade-off is maturity, not security. The interface is plain, the mobile side is very new, and some users report slow support and billing hiccups. You are trading polish and a settled mobile experience for price and solid zero-knowledge encryption.
Android is the concrete form of that trade. The iOS app arrived on 10 August 2026; twenty-seven days later, on 6 September 2026, there was still no Android app. Passpack's own Downloads menu offered only iOS and the browser extension, and a Google Play search for 'passpack' that day returned thirteen apps, all of them rival password managers and none of them this one. If your team is on Android, plan as though the app does not exist, because it does not.
Their own pages lag their announcements, too, though less than they did. Passpack told partners on 2 September 2026 that TOTP now works on every plan, and on 3 September the word appeared on neither the plans nor the key-features page; by 6 September the plans comparison table lists both TOTP and 'Mobile app for iOS', in the section that carries no plan exclusions. The key-features page has not caught up: on 6 September it still listed 'Mobile & Browser Extensions' under New Features Coming Soon, four weeks after iOS shipped and with the extensions already sold on the plans page. Read the plans table rather than the newsletter, and confirm stored TOTP codes inside the 28-day trial.

video:video.video:title: Payoneer Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The conversion and cross-currency withdrawal markups are where it quietly costs you: for pure currency conversion a specialist like Wise is often cheaper. Payoneer earns its keep on marketplace payouts and getting paid by international clients, less so as an FX tool.

video:video.video:title: PhotoGenerator Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The credit is not a picture, and that is the thing to understand before buying. Starter's 360 monthly credits are 360 images on GPT Image 2.5 Flare at 1 credit each, 180 on Nano Banana at 2, 120 on GPT Image 2 at 3 or 45 on Nano Banana Pro at 8, and on video, 90 clips on Seedance Pro at 4 credits, 18 on Seedance 2.0 at 20, 7 on Veo 3.1 Fast and 3 on Veo 3.1 Quality. The headline counts ('Up to 360 images', 'Up to 90 videos') are the cheapest model in each column; they reconcile with the vendor's own table, but they are still the cheapest models.
The Yearly toggle advertises 30% OFF. Every yearly plan carries exactly twelve months of credits, so the saving is the price cut alone: 16.7% on Starter, 17.2% to 21.5% on Pro and 25.2% to 30.1% on Max, which means only the 14,400-credit Max reaches the badge. The Pay Once packs are dearer per credit than any subscription and, despite the 'pay once' framing, expire after 360 days and cannot be refunded.
One naming quirk: Seedance Pro costs 4 credits while Seedance 2.0 costs 20 and Seedance 2.0 Fast 15, so the model called Pro is the cheapest of the three, not the dearest.
And know what you are buying: an aggregator, not a model. You pay for one workspace, one balance and one prompt gallery across other companies' models, so the question is whether that convenience beats going to those providers directly at your volume.

video:video.video:title: Piktochart Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The ladder here is not about how much you make, it is about which file you are allowed to hand over. Pro, the tier the page marks most popular, exports PNG only. PDF and PowerPoint are Business features, which the full feature table confirms in a single row most people scroll past. So if the reason you want this is to email a PDF handout or drop slides into a deck, Pro at $10 a member a month is not a cheaper Piktochart: it is the wrong product. Your real entry price is $17 a member a month on annual billing, or $20 monthly.
The free plan reads as generous and is not. Unlimited projects, two downloads, and not two a month: the comparison table lists the number of downloads as a flat 2. In our test on 20 October 2026 that counter ran per account, not per design: 2, then 1, then 0 across two different designs, and the third try opened 'You have run out of free downloads.' That is enough to find out whether you like the editor, which is a fair trial, but it is not the working free tier some competitors in this category offer, so do not plan around it.
The third thing to price is the AI credits: 60 on Free, 500 on Pro, 1,000 on Business. The pricing page does not say what one credit buys or what happens when you run out. The app says more, but not all of it: in our test on 20 October 2026 the AI infographic button said 1 credit, yet the free balance went from 60 to 57 after two failed attempts and one that worked, and the app sold one-off top-up packs from $20 for 2,000 credits. If AI generation is the reason you are buying, try it on Free first and watch the counter, because that meter can decide your bill.
One last piece of arithmetic. The annual discount is 33% on Pro but only 15% on Business, so the saving shrinks exactly at the tier most teams that need PDF or PowerPoint end up on. And if you have an educational email address or nonprofit status the picture changes completely: Education is $39.99 per member for a whole year and Nonprofit is $60, against $120 for

video:video.video:title: Pippit Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The meter is credits per attempt, not per usable result, and buyer reviews centre on exactly that. Trustpilot reviewers describe generations that failed but still consumed their credits, refunds that were hard to get, and support replies measured in weeks. A tool that charges for its own failures puts the cost of unreliability on you.

video:video.video:title: Pixlr Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
Pixlr does not refund a processed payment, and monthly AI credits do not accumulate: they are reset to the plan allowance at each renewal and fall to zero when you cancel. The credit estimates are generous for fast models and much thinner for the better ones; Premium's 1,000 credits are about 200 pro images by Pixlr's own table. Ultra's unlimited fast generation is subject to fair use, and the page says availability is not guaranteed. The free version carries ads and a daily save limit Pixlr does not quantify. Upgrading is not possible on a PayPal subscription. Prices here were read in euros; buyers elsewhere see their own currency.
The pricing FAQ and the Terms of Use contradict each other on credits. The FAQ says credit packs never expire; the terms, last updated 13 May 2026, say purchased credits are valid for one year from purchase and then expire automatically, and are non-refundable. The pricing page says yearly subscribers get all their credits valid for a year; the terms say all plan credits are provided monthly and any unused at the end of the month expire. Until Pixlr aligns the two, plan as if the stricter terms apply: use packs within a year and do not count on carrying yearly credits from one month to the next.
The terms also let Pixlr change the price, package or features of a plan at any time, with or without notice. Publishing AI-generated content on Pixlr's platform grants Pixlr an irrevocable, royalty-free, worldwide licence to it, so keep client work you have not released off its community features. Disputes go to arbitration in Singapore, where Pixlr Pte Ltd is based.

video:video.video:title: Pricefy Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Credit where due: the free tier is real. But the paid ladder rises fast — Starter at $49 buys only 100 SKUs, and repricing itself waits for Pro at $99 — and price updates run at most twice a day even on Enterprise, so this is rules-based repricing, not marketplace-speed. The headline prices are monthly rates; the advertised savings require annual commitment.

video:video.video:title: PulseMonitor Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The refund policy is strict: monthly and yearly fees are non-refundable, including the unused part of a year, so the $90 annual plan is a commitment. Neither the terms nor the refund policy name the company behind PulseMonitor or the country whose law applies; the terms say only the jurisdiction in which we operate. The free plan checks every 5 minutes and alerts only by email, Discord and Telegram, while Slack, PagerDuty, status pages and cron heartbeats need Pro. The SEO analyzer is a one-click site audit, not rank tracking. We have not used PulseMonitor ourselves. The 'Last updated' line on the terms, refund and security pages read 14 October 2026 when we read them on 14 October and 25 October 2026 when we read them on 25 October, so it follows the day of reading and does not tell you when the wording last changed. The terms cap liability at the greater of the fees paid in the previous 12 months or $100, and say PulseMonitor has no obligation to keep your data after termination. PagerDuty alerts need Zapier or your own proxy.

video:video.video:title: PushOwl Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The bundles are push-first: every paid tier still caps included email at 500 a month, so 'omnichannel' email at any real volume means buying separate credits, and consumption-based pricing gets harder to predict as your sends climb. It's also Shopify-exclusive, so it becomes a dead end the day you move platforms.

video:video.video:title: Pythago Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Pythago bills per store, so every store you add adds a full subscription and the bill scales linearly: ten stores is $390 a month, twenty is $780, and there is no enterprise step that flattens the curve. The rate does improve with volume ($59 for one store, $49 each at two, $39 each from three up) so price the trajectory rather than this month’s bill. The $39 on the 3+ card is not an entry price; one store is $59, which the vendor now states plainly in its hero and its FAQ.

video:video.video:title: QuickSigner Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The price is the argument, and the legal ceiling is the limit. QuickSigner's own llms.txt says it issues Advanced, not Qualified, Electronic Signatures, and names its weaker fit plainly: organisations needing QES, contract lifecycle management with redlining and analytics, or on-premise deployment. Below that line it does what it says for a fraction of per-envelope pricing: recipients sign from a link with no account, app or token. A few users report occasional email-deliverability hiccups, which weighs more here than usual because the emailed link is the whole signing route.

video:video.video:title: ReachStream Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The meter is on exporting, not on looking, and that is the number to size before you pick a tier. Contact and company views are unlimited on every plan including the free one, so the demo will feel generous; what you actually pay for is pulling those records out, and separately for revealing an email address, which is a second meter the plan cards do not put next to the first. Free gives 100 exports and 200 email views a month, which is a sample rather than a workflow. The second thing to check is seats: Starter and Pro both include exactly one, so a two-person sales team is on Business at $99 a month before it needs the extra credits. Credits do not roll over: the FAQ, re-read on 19 September 2026, says unused credits reset at the start of each new billing cycle, so a plan sized for a busy month is simply wasted in a quiet one. That same question answered the other way on 10 September, which is reason enough to check it yourself before you commit. Underbuying is no clearer either: two figures on the page are not explained anywhere: Starter and Pro promise to "unlock an extra $250 / $500 worth of data", which is priced in dollars rather than in credits or records, and the cost of a credit once you run out is not published at all.

video:video.video:title: Reclaim.ai Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The magic only works on a calendar it can write to. Google Calendar was first, but Microsoft 365, Outlook.com and Exchange-backed accounts are supported too (reclaim.ai/integrations/outlook-calendar, read 15 September 2026); Reclaim's own help centre still lists hosted and on-premise Exchange as unsupported. The free tier is quite limited. A genuine time-saver for the right setup, useless for the wrong one.

video:video.video:title: Restream Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The channel caps are the business model -- each tier buys a few more destinations. Seats are the second meter: Free and Standard include one and cannot buy another at all, while Professional and Business include two and sell extras at $25 a month. Price it at your real destination count and team size, not the sticker.

video:video.video:title: Retouch4me Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Work out which lane you are in before you pay, because the three lanes price the same photo very differently. One plugin forever at $145 is honest value, but a working portrait stack means four plugins at $145-$179 each, $648 in total, while the Start subscription hands you the entire set for $169 a year with 2,400 retouches included. The catch cuts the other way too: own-forever versus keep-paying is the real decision, since the credits' 5-year rollover only holds 'while the subscription is active' — stop paying and the suite and the stockpile are gone. Low volume? Cloud retouching without a subscription is sold in packs, $24 for 100 retouches, and at $0.15 to $0.24 a photo it is the dearest lane per image, not the cheapest.

video:video.video:title: Riverside Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The meter is not recording time, it is separate-track download time, and separate tracks are the entire reason to use this rather than a video call. Recording itself is unlimited. Their own FAQ on hitting the cap: you can still access your content but cannot download new separate tracks until the next billing cycle or you upgrade. So a busy interview month does not cost you more money, it quietly stops you delivering, which is worse. Fifteen hours on Pro is about seven or eight hour-long interviews once you count retakes and the recording that runs while you set up. There is a 14-day trial rather than a published free plan.

video:video.video:title: RocketReach Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The published prices are annual rates, and the annual term is doing more work than the page lets on. RocketReach's own feature table lists searches as unlimited on the annual term but caps them at 100, 250 and 1,000 a month if you bill monthly, and caps exports at those same numbers instead of 1,200, 3,600 and 20,000 a year. So the $19 on the card is $229 up front, and the flexible-looking monthly option is the one that rations the product. Their FAQ adds that cancelling takes effect from the next term, so a year is a year.
The plan boundary matters more than the price. Essentials is email only: mobile and direct phone numbers start at Pro, and so do the Salesforce, Outreach, Salesloft and Bullhorn integrations, technographics and org charts. Above Ultimate the ladder stops being a ladder, with enterprise starting at $6K annually against $1,379 for Ultimate.
And the numbers that sell it are all RocketReach's own, printed on their pricing page: 700 million professionals, 60 million companies, 98% accuracy, 30 million users, 95% of the S&P 500. We have measured none of them. Contact-data accuracy is the thing that varies most by territory and by seniority, and a database claim is an average, not a promise about your list. The free account is the right answer to that: it costs nothing and needs no card, so run the free lookups against a slice of your own target accounts before you commit to a year. A lookup that finds nothing verified is refunded, per their FAQ, which makes that test cheaper still.

video:video.video:title: SEO Space Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Squarespace has been quietly absorbing the job this tool was invented for. The platform's own SEO panel, checklist, sitemaps and structured data are free, and its AI-suggested titles, descriptions and alt text are available on Fluid Engine 7.1. On 7 July 2026 it announced AI Visibility, brand tracking across AI search, included on 7.1 plans with no extra subscription. It is metered against plan-varying AI credits rather than unlimited. If you own a single Squarespace site, a large share of what you would pay for here is now a friendlier wrapper around something the platform already does.
