The tool earns its keep on volume and client work, not on one site. Note too what the disclaimer under their own plan cards says out loud — “All plans include every feature. No artificial restrictions.” — so moving up the ladder buys site slots, not a better tool. One thing arrived after that promise, though: Orbit, a five-agent AI layer added since August, sits on its own card as a second subscription at $119 a month or $952 a year (read 16 September and 4 October 2026), so the feature that is currently being marketed hardest is the one no plan includes.

video:video.video:title: SEOmatic Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
This app is eleven years old and has 151 reviews (28 September 2026; it was 114 in August). That is the number to sit with. On the same listing page Shopify shows three direct rivals. On 28 September 2026 SEOLab stood at 4.9 over 2,752 reviews, TinySEO at 5.0 over 2,518 and Smart SEO at 5.0 over 956; in our August reading SEOLab was free, Tiny SEO free to install and Smart SEO had a free plan. All three carry between six and eighteen times the review volume, all are rated higher, and none of them charges by product count. SEOmatic's 4.4 is a real rating from real merchants, but it is the weakest track record on its own page.
The distribution behind that 4.4 matters too: 81% five stars against 7% one star, with almost nothing in the middle. The most substantial recent review, from March 2025, is a merchant of six months saying it appears to work on images and nothing else, and that support is difficult and slow. The vendor replied that the reports do exist, and asked them to get in touch. An older one-star from a merchant who lasted seventeen minutes reads 'Paid for it to tell me 0% savings'. Both are about the same thing: what the app actually did after installation was not visible to the person paying for it.
And the product cap is a hard ceiling, not a soft one. There is no tier above 5,000 products on the listing or on seomatic.io, so if your catalogue is larger than that, the published ladder simply does not have a row for you.

video:video.video:title: Salesflare Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's deliberately lean: no built-in dialer, no quoting or invoicing, and reporting feels basic unless you export. Integrations cover the essentials (Gmail, Outlook, Zapier) but niche tools lean on Zapier, and at higher seat counts the price overlaps fuller CRMs. Two further limits come from Salesflare's own help centre. Microsoft 365 users who send campaigns can land on Microsoft's restricted-users list: the article updated 17 September 2026 says this happens when a mailbox exceeds its sending limit or is flagged by spam filters, that Salesflare's own quotas do not always prevent it, and that an admin then has to unblock the user in the Microsoft 365 Defender portal. And the no-limits promise has a fair-use edge, set out in the record-limits article.

video:video.video:title: Salesflow Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The per-seat rate falls with team size but the monthly bill does not follow it: 19 seats on Starter is $1,330 while 20 seats on Pro is $799, so a team that stops one seat short of a tier pays $531 a month more for less. The same cliff sits at 49-to-50 seats and again at 99-to-100. And the monthly quotas are the real ceiling: 400 invites and 800 Open InMails is a fixed budget, not a starting point.

video:video.video:title: SaneBox Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It works with any email provider, which is a genuine advantage over the built-in tools in Gmail and Outlook. But you are paying monthly to filter mail that modern clients increasingly sort for free. The value is real only if your inbox is overwhelming and native filters are not cutting it. Price it on the plan you would actually keep: the headline rate is a two-year commitment, and month to month the same Snack plan is $9.49 rather than $4.54.

video:video.video:title: Scrolly Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The two features carry very different risk, the app presents them as one install, and since August the money has been split across them in a way the name does not warn you about. Infinite scroll replaces the paginated collection URLs a crawler uses to walk a large catalogue, pushes your footer permanently out of reach, and on some themes collides with the load-more or filtering logic already in the theme: that is a merchandising decision, not a styling toggle. The app also edits Online Store script tags and the theme, so it adds a third-party script to every page and an uninstall can leave remnants.
What changed is which half you pay for. Re-read on 2 November 2026, the free plan keeps the scroll-to-top button and infinite scroll sits on the $4.99 Unlimited plan ($2.99 in September), where on 25 August the whole app was free. The amount is trivial; the shape is not. The half that can quietly alter how your collection pages are crawled is now the half with a billing relationship behind it, and the seven-day trial is the only window in which you will find out what it does to your store before the charge starts. Anything written about this app before September, including a free-forever recommendation, describes an install that no longer exists.

video:video.video:title: Seamless.ai Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Data accuracy is the recurring complaint: independent tests put email deliverability around 74% (20–30% bounce) versus ZoomInfo's ~2–3%, so real cost per usable contact climbs. The buying experience is the other weak spot: sales-led, auto-renew with 30–60 day written cancellation, and reports of charges after a 'confirmed' cancellation.

video:video.video:title: Section Library Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
Almost three years on the App Store and one review. The app launched 10 October 2023 and, as of 5 October 2026, exactly one merchant has written about it: a five-star note from October 2023 by someone who had it installed for four minutes. That is not evidence of quality and not evidence of trouble: it is an absence of evidence, and on an app that writes sections into your live theme, that absence is the main thing to weigh. On the same listing page Shopify shows Section Store with 2,967 reviews (read 5 October 2026), also free to install, which is what a track record looks like in this category. And on 17 September and again on 5 October 2026 the vendor’s own site, sectionlibrary.com, answered with Shopify’s “Store unavailable” page instead of a website.
Second, the credit is undefined. Every plan is priced in credits and nothing on the listing says what one buys, so you cannot price your own usage before you commit.
Third, the AI half of the product is Google's. Sections are generated by Gemini 3.1 Pro, so output quality and consistency shift when Google ships a new model, which is outside the vendor's hands as much as yours. The library half, the 200+ pre-built sections, is the part that depends on nobody else, and it is the part worth judging the app on.

video:video.video:title: Securify Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Blocking by country and IP is a blunt instrument and it cuts both ways: every rule that keeps out a fraudster also keeps out a customer travelling, using a corporate VPN, or living behind a carrier NAT. The app is honest enough to give you a live log of what it blocked, and that log is the part to actually read: a rule set nobody reviews quietly costs sales. Also worth separating in your head: blocking bots from your analytics is a reporting fix, while blocking fraud at checkout is a money fix, and the two need different rules.

video:video.video:title: Seel Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two things to weigh, and neither is the price you pay, because you do not pay one. First, you cannot set the fee. Seel's algorithm prices it, so if it lands too high for your niche and shoppers stop opting in, your only lever is switching the feature off entirely. Second, the charge appears on your checkout, not Seel's: shopper-side complaints filed with the BBB describe the fee arriving in the cart with the opt-out easy to miss, and that lands on your brand. Test it as a customer before you enable it. Also check the platform list: Shopify, BigCommerce and Adobe Commerce only, with no WooCommerce, Wix or custom storefront support.

video:video.video:title: Seele Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
You cannot know in advance what a game will cost. Koins are deducted by the AI time, cloud time and third-party tools a task uses, and the help centre says every change you ask for, from renaming a character to fixing a bug, is a new generation that costs Koins again. It also says Unity projects cost significantly more than lightweight Three.js web games. The 360 free Koins are meant for a first build, and one public review we read, from a 16-year-old, says he ran out before finishing his first game.
The cheapest plan does not let you sell what you make. Commercial use is listed on Pro and Ultra only, and the terms (section 4.2, updated 28 July 2026) say the right to publish, sell or advertise in your games comes with an active subscription at Pro or above, which is $50 a month or $39 billed annually. On Standard at $20 you can build and share, not earn.
The pricing page and the terms disagree on the two things that protect your money. The upgrade page FAQ says unused Koins roll over and the help centre says they never expire, while the terms say unused subscription Koins do not carry over to the next billing period. The upgrade page advertises a 7-day free trial and a 7-day money-back guarantee, while the terms say all payments are final and non-refundable, and that refunds may be refused for anything bought with a coupon or discount, which covers the 50% first-month offer the page applies by default. The terms also say a chargeback raised without first emailing support will be treated as fraud. Finally, the homepage promises you can take your Unity project with you, while the help centre's article on Koins says source code download is currently not available. We have not used the product.
The export picture has moved since we first read it. Seele's guide, read on 27 October 2026, tells you to switch to the files view to review, download or export the project, and lists Three.js, Unity, Godot and Unreal as target engines, with typical output ranging from a playa

video:video.video:title: Selixer Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
Read the feature lists rather than the prices and the entry tier stops looking like the product. Essence at $149 a month gives you two seats, one connected ad platform, a year of history and an inventory health score. The full True Profit waterfall, the per-product P&L and the POAS and CAC tracking, the reason anyone installs a profit dashboard, all start on Catalyst at $299. So the real price of what this app is sold on is double the headline.
The ad-platform caps decide the tier as much as the features do: one, then two, then three. If you run Meta, Google and TikTok you are on the $399 plan for connectivity alone, whatever your revenue looks like.
The monthly figure is also not the whole bill. Each plan carries an AI credit allowance (500, 2,000 and 3,000) and the listing sells top-ups from $25, with usage-based charges billed on the same 30-day cycle. Find out what spends a credit before you budget around the headline.
And this is a new app. It launched on 19 May 2026 and has one public review. There is nothing bad in the record, but there is barely any record, and this is a tool you hand your cost prices, your ad spend and your margins to. Use the 14-day trial to reconcile its numbers against a month you have already closed in your own books before you trust a dashboard you cannot yet audit.

video:video.video:title: Sellfy Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest mechanic is the revenue ladder: plans cap by your ANNUAL SALES, so success moves you up. But the caps are soft - Sellfy's FAQ says it may charge 2% on revenue above your limit rather than forcing an upgrade, so ask whether that applies to you before jumping a tier. The 0% transaction fee is rare and beats percentage-taking platforms at volume; below a few hundred in monthly sales the flat subscription is the tax instead, and your processor still takes about 2.9% + 30c regardless.

video:video.video:title: Serpstat Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The thing you are actually buying is data coverage, and that is the one thing you cannot verify: Serpstat's own published figures do not agree with each other. Re-read on 24 July 2026, their homepage says 529 billion backlinks, their data hub says 1.1 trillion, and their backlinks page says 1.7 trillion in the prose while its own spec block on that same page says 1.1 trillion. The keyword count reads 8.62 billion on one page and 7.46 billion on another. That is not evidence the data is thin; it is evidence that these numbers cannot serve as a basis for your decision. Judge it on your own searches during the trial instead. Two other things to weigh. Backlink reports are capped at 10,000 results per report on Team, Team x2 and Agency alike, so paying from $129 to $499 buys more of everything except a deeper backlink report. And 'maximum pages to scan' in a single crawl (5,000 / 25,000 / 50,000) is a far smaller number than the monthly 'pages to audit' allowance it sits next to.

video:video.video:title: Shipdock Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
Read the carrier list against your own country before anything else. The listing slug is 'packeta', the developer is happyapps.cz, and cash-on-delivery tracking is a headline feature: all three point at Central and Eastern Europe, where Packeta and Zásilkovna are everyday carriers and COD is a normal way to pay. More than twenty carriers are supported, but a US or UK merchant should confirm theirs is among them before the five-day trial starts.
The second thing is the trial length against the job. Five days on Lite and Basic is short for a shipping integration, because the test that matters is a real order going out with a real label to a real address. Install it on a day you are actually shipping, not on a quiet Sunday.

video:video.video:title: Shorby Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: In a category where the market leader has a generous free plan, Shorby charges from day one, so it has to earn the gap. Its case rests on two differentiated features: messenger deep-links, one tap into WhatsApp/Telegram chats, and retargeting pixels firing on every click. If you use neither, Linktree's free tier wins; if messenger-first selling or ad retargeting is your funnel, the $15 pays for itself.

video:video.video:title: Signeasy Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The $10 Personal plan is annual-billed and single-seat, and note that sign-unlimited is not send-unlimited: proper unlimited sending starts at Business, $20 per seat on a yearly commitment, while contract-management features gate at Business Pro, $30 per seat.

video:video.video:title: SimplyBook.me Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The plan ladder is set by bookings per month and by how many custom features you may switch on, and those two ceilings move independently, so you can outgrow a plan on features while nowhere near the booking cap, or the reverse. Free and Basic also carry SimplyBook.me branding on your booking page; white-label starts at Premium. Two integration limits sit in their own documentation. Calendar Sync works with web calendars only, and the help page warns it may not work with Microsoft Exchange calendars. The Zapier connector, which gained a create-booking action in June 2026, stops working once HIPAA or Google Authenticator is switched on, so the practices most likely to need HIPAA lose the Zapier route.

video:video.video:title: Smartli Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
Smartli bundles nine AI tools (copy, SEO, images, logos) into one suite, and that breadth is also the honest catch: each individual tool is competent rather than best-in-class, so a team that leans hard on one job may outgrow it toward a specialist. And like all AI copy, its product descriptions and ad copy need a human edit and a fact-check: never publish specs or claims it invents about your product. For a store that wants many content jobs handled cheaply in one place, it's efficient.
Two places tell different stories about trying it for free. The Shopify App Store listing, read on 27 October 2026, says 'Free plan available' and shows a Free card that lists only 24/7 chat support, while smartli.ai/pricing shows four paid tiers and no free plan on either tab. A one-star review from an Australian store, edited 24 July 2024, says the advertised free account was not offered after installing and the app would not allow a test without choosing a plan. If a free tier matters to you, check which plan the app selects before you approve the Shopify charge.
The star average hides a split. Of 66 ratings, 53 are five stars and 4 are one star (4.0 overall), and the one- and two-star reviews are nearly all about billing rather than writing quality: a charge after cancelling inside the trial (May 2023), the free-account complaint above, and the November 2025 review about a $152 charge on the install day. Smartli's terms add that a failed monthly payment may be retried on the same card until you cancel or change the payment method in your account settings, so an expired card does not end the subscription.

video:video.video:title: SocialBee Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: You are billed per social profile, not per person, and a profile is one brand account on one network. A single business posting to Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, X and TikTok has used the whole Bootstrap allowance before a second brand or a client exists. The second thing is that people cost extra on top: Bootstrap and Accelerate are single-user plans, so a two-person team on eight profiles is $49 plus $10, not $29. Count your profiles across every network first: that number, not your team size, decides the tier.

video:video.video:title: Spocket Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Spocket's pitch is faster-shipping US and EU suppliers, and that's real, but you still pay twice: the monthly subscription and the wholesale product cost, so margins depend on picking items with room to mark up. Catalog breadth is narrower than giant AliExpress-based tools (that's the trade for vetting and shipping speed), and the low Starter product cap pushes serious stores up to Pro quickly. It reduces, not removes, the usual dropshipping risks.

video:video.video:title: Stampezee Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The category is honest and proven (digital stamp cards beat lost paper cards), and the platform is young with limited public review coverage, so use the 14-day trial on a paid plan to run one real campaign and measure repeat-visit lift before the first charge, because the refund policy excludes changes of mind and unused plan periods. The deeper truth of loyalty programs: the mechanics are 10% of the outcome; a reward worth returning for is the other 90%.

video:video.video:title: StoreLock Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
Be clear about which half of the app you are paying for. The copy protection blocks right-click, text selection, keyboard shortcuts and image dragging, and the vendor's own FAQ says what it cannot stop: screenshots, browser developer tools, visitors with JavaScript switched off and automated scrapers, which is how stores actually get cloned. It is a deterrent against casual copying. The part that does real work is detection and takedown: clone detection, a nightly scan of hundreds of lookalike variants of your domain that a person at StoreLock reviews before you get an alert, reverse image searches, and DMCA and abuse notices pre-filled with the evidence. Even then, the FAQ says StoreLock cannot make a registrar respond, and a typical notice takes days to weeks.
The gap between the plans is large. On Premium at $19 you file the notices yourself; having StoreLock's team watch the alerts and file for you is the Enterprise plan at $399 a month, about twenty times the price. Most of the reviews thank 'Adam and his team' by name for chasing fakes down, so check before you install which plan the help you are reading about came with. Today image monitoring is $0.20 per monitored image on the Shopify listing: ten images scanned weekly is about 40 scans, or $8 a month. The FAQ we read on 27 October 2026 already quotes the StoreLock 2 terms instead (100 scans included on Premium, then $0.05 each), so check in the app which rate your plan is billed at.
The one critical review is a warning about putting a script in front of your storefront. On 28 April 2026 a Canadian store that had used the app for about a year wrote that after an update everyone was blocked from accessing their store, and they removed it rather than wait a day for support. StoreLock replied that it had released an update to its content protection, had no other such reports, had received no support request and had contacted the store within 30 minutes of the uninstall. The other 9 of 10 reviews are five star

video:video.video:title: StoreSEO Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Know what an SEO app can and cannot do before you buy any tier. This one fixes the mechanical layer well: meta titles and descriptions in bulk, alt text, compressed images, JSON-LD, sitemaps, indexing requests, and none of that creates demand for products nobody is searching for. It is maintenance, not marketing, and on a catalogue of 25 products the free tier already does most of it. Two specifics worth a raised eyebrow. The pricing gap between Essential at $39.99 for 250 products and Advanced at $249.99 for 10,000 is filled by a $99.99 Growth plan. That plan lives on the vendor's own site but not on the App Store listing our link points to, which is a strange place to hide a tier. And the AEO/GEO features: the LLMs.txt generator, the Agents.md editor, the separate “agentic” ranking: are a bet, not a channel. No major search or AI vendor has committed to reading llms.txt, so treat those numbers as a hypothesis you are testing rather than traffic you are buying.

video:video.video:title: Storylane Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The jump from Starter to Growth is $50 to $625 a month (twelve and a half times) and the free tier is capped at one live demo, so the moment you want a second demo published you are on the ladder. What is actually being sold at each step is visitor de-anonymisation: 250 a month on Starter, 2,500 on Growth, 10,000 on Premium. Price that against what you already pay a separate tool to do, because it is the meter that decides your tier, not the number of demos. Extra seats are charged on top at $40 to $100 each, which means a five-person sales team on Starter is not $50 a month, it is $210.

video:video.video:title: Streak Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The pitch, CRM living inside Gmail, is also the ceiling: everything happens in the inbox, which power users love and growing teams outgrow (reporting, permissions, cross-team process). And note the trajectory: the free tier is gone and per-seat prices sit at real-CRM levels now, so the 'lightweight Gmail add-on' framing no longer matches the invoice. If the inbox is where your deals live, few tools feel this natural.

video:video.video:title: Success.co Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The ladder rewards size rather than commitment: each band's rate applies only to the seats inside it, so the 26th user costs a dollar less than the 25th, and the annual discount is worth about the same single dollar per user. So the number that decides your bill is headcount, not billing term, and at the small end, where most teams start, $12 a user is the least favourable rate on the whole page. The two capabilities a security team will ask for first, SSO and SCIM, are not in any plan: they are $250 a month each, which on a 20-person account doubles the bill.

video:video.video:title: SupaEasy Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two things the marketing glosses over. First, the 'free' plan is development-stores only, so any live use is paid, and the AI generator that headlines the app is not in Premium ($49) but in Advanced ($99), plus AI credits bought separately ($25 per 50), so the AI promise realistically costs $99+ a month. Second, the rating is suspiciously spotless: 5.0 across 233 reviews, all five-star, on the App Store listing on 29 September 2026, and the praise dwells on fast human support (Andrea, Fabio) more than on the no-code AI running unattended, which hints the tool can need hand-holding.

video:video.video:title: Survicate Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The plan is metered by response volume, not by surveys: a viral NPS month can push you a tier up, and the free plan's 30-day retention quietly deletes your history. Mind the billing asymmetry too: Starter is monthly-only while Growth and up expect an annual commitment.

video:video.video:title: Tapita AI SEO Blog Builder Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
Publishing volume is the trap this tool makes cheap. It generates posts quickly and schedules them daily or weekly in bulk, and a Shopify blog filled with unedited AI articles is precisely the pattern search engines have spent the last two years demoting: the app lowers the cost of production, not the bar for ranking. Used the other way round, as a drafting and structuring tool for posts you actually edit, it is sensible.
The price is the second thing to watch, and on 19 September 2026 there is none to read. The listing publishes no plan block and gives its pricing as Free. That is not the same as free being the whole story: the features it advertises (AI generation, bulk creation, translation, scheduling) were metered in credits until August, and no credit allowance or overage rate is stated anywhere on the page now. The same developer's other listing still prints a complete ladder, so this one is not simply a developer who does not publish prices. Go in expecting to ask what the limits are, and do not plan a content calendar around an allowance nobody has told you the size of.

video:video.video:title: Tax1099 Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Per-form pricing is cheap for a handful of 1099s, but it's metered: TIN matching, W-9 requests, state filing and corrections can each carry their own charge. A business filing across many recipients and states should tally the add-ons, not just the headline per-form rate. It's a filing tool, not a bookkeeping system; it assumes your payee data is already clean.

video:video.video:title: TaxCycle Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: This is professional preparer software priced for firms, not a consumer filing app: the cost only makes sense if you're preparing returns for clients at volume. The suites start at about CAD $1,655 a year for one user and each extra seat adds several hundred dollars, so a two- or three-person practice should budget the suite price plus seats, plus GST or HST, before comparing it with per-return alternatives.

video:video.video:title: Team Pulse Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The tiers gate on TWO axes at once (member count and project/pipeline count) so you can hit a wall on either. The CRM pipeline is a big part of the pitch, but it doesn't exist below the $79 Growth plan (Free and Starter have none), and member limits are tight: Starter is a single seat, Growth just three. The headline rates are the annual ones; month-to-month costs 25 to 34% more ($39 against $29 on Starter, $99 against $79 on Growth).

video:video.video:title: Teikametrics Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
Read the Advanced tier carefully, because it is not a subscription: it is a subscription plus a percentage. Three per cent of ad spend above $10,000 means a seller spending $40,000 a month pays an extra $900 on top of whatever the custom base is, and that line scales with the thing the product is supposed to make more efficient. That is not automatically wrong, it aligns them with your growth, but it does mean your bill rises when your advertising does, and you should model it at your expected spend rather than your current one. The $10K threshold is the number to watch: crossing it changes the pricing model, not just the price.
The 3% does not stop when the subscription does. The billing article says that even after cancellation you still incur the 3% monthly charge on any ad spend over $10K unless your connected merchants are removed, and that removal is done by contacting support; the same applies on the free Basic plan you are moved to when you cancel. A seller who cancels at $30,000 a month of ad spend and forgets the merchant connection keeps paying $600 a month for a plan it no longer uses.
The two official price lists disagree above $10K. The pricing page shows Advanced as custom pricing plus 3%; the help article prices Advanced at $1,199 to $1,439 a month without mentioning the 3%, and adds an Essentials Tier 2 at $499 to $599 plus 3% that the pricing page does not list. Get the tier name, the base fee and the percentage in writing before you connect an account that spends more than $10K.
The contract terms are written for a fixed term. Orders renew automatically for the same length unless you give written notice (email is enough) at least 15 days before the term ends; the customer has no right to terminate for convenience, and ending early means paying the fees for the rest of the term within 30 days. Late invoices can carry 1.5% interest a month, and disputes go to the courts of Massachusetts. Only Essentials can be cancelled on the billing page; on Ad

video:video.video:title: Tellent Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Tellent's modular shape is useful (you can buy just the ATS, or just the HRIS) but nothing is priced in public: every tier on tellent.com/pricing ends in 'Get a demo' (read in a browser on 9 September 2026), and recruitee.com/pricing carries no figures either. Ask for Start, Advance and Optimize quoted together with their renewal prices, because you have no anchor to check a single number against. And as with every ATS, workflow fit (approval chains, careers-site needs, integrations with your assessment tools) matters more than the feature list; the free trial is enough to run one real vacancy through, so do that.

video:video.video:title: Tenable Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Note on how we link this one, updated 28 Jul 2026: between 21 and 28 July our partner link was dead: Tenable's shop subdomain stopped resolving, so we pointed the link at Tenable's own product page and earned nothing from it. Tenable confirmed on 28 July that the links are repaired; we re-tested them that day and the link now works again, lands on the same Nessus product page, and does pay us a commission. This is serious, enterprise-grade security tooling with an enterprise price and a learning curve, not a set-and-forget scanner. You need someone who can act on the findings, or you're paying for reports nobody reads.

video:video.video:title: TestDriver.ai Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
You do not control your own seat count. The pricing page says a seat is billed automatically for every GitHub user who gets a pull-request review or runs a test, so the bill is set by who touches your repository, not by a number you chose. On a team of ten that is $240 a month before a single test has run, and it scales with contributors rather than with usage.
The allowance improved in the repricing we read on 2 November 2026: 360 testing minutes at the published $0.08 overage rate is $28.80 of metered value against a $24 seat. But the meter still runs on sandbox uptime rather than test duration: the clock covers booting the machine and loading your app, not only the part where it clicks things. A suite that takes eight minutes of wall time per pull request exhausts 360 minutes in 45 pull requests.
The FAQ now says your plan includes 360 testing minutes each billing period, which reads as one allowance for the plan rather than 360 per seat. Budget it that way: on a ten-person team the gap between 360 and 3,600 minutes is $259.20 a month at $0.08. And note that charges, including the one when the trial converts, are non-refundable.
One coverage trap: if you ship a Mac desktop app, or anything on iOS or Android, Pro does not cover you. Those platforms are marked coming soon and sit under Enterprise, which is quote-only.
What is good here is the part that usually breaks. Tests are written against what a user does rather than against selectors: the generated file reads `td.find("signup button").click()` and `td.assert("dashboard is visible")`, and the documentation tells you to describe behaviour instead of implementation, which is the opposite of the brittle CSS-selector suites this category is famous for. That is also the risk: an element resolved by an AI from a description can drift for reasons a diff will not show you.

video:video.video:title: TheTop Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The price is the knock, because there isn't one. TheTop publishes no rate of any kind: no list price, no per-seat figure, no percentage, and no pricing page: we checked on 19 September 2026 and the old one returns a 404. Everything runs through Book a demo, so the first number you hear will be quoted to you, with your own AI spend already on the table. That is a weak position to negotiate from, and it is worth asking for the basis (flat platform fee, per request, or a share of measured savings) before you show anyone your invoice.
The savings claim is measured by the vendor, against a baseline the vendor computes. The site says eligible traffic is priced against your own baseline and shows 22% and 43% saved in its examples, but the party doing the measuring is also the party being paid. Ask how baseline is defined, which traffic counts as eligible, and whether you can audit the calculation: a reuse or reroute that quietly swaps a frontier model for a cheaper one also changes the output, and only your own evaluation will tell you whether that trade was worth it.
One more thing to weigh: this product sits in the request path. The Engine applies memory, caching, routing and policy before traffic reaches the model, which is exactly where the savings come from and also exactly where an outage or a bad routing rule lands on every AI feature you run. The vendor's answer is that you start read-only and move traffic when you choose, which is the right shape, but the day you point production at it, a middle layer has become a dependency.

video:video.video:title: Thordata Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Everything is a meter (per GB, per IP, per 1K responses) so the bill scales with usage. And every rate the site advertises is the largest package on its ladder: $0.65 a GB means buying 5,000 GB, while 1 GB of the same product costs $2.00. Budget at your own volume, not at the headline. Plus the category-wide caveat we'd give any residential-proxy vendor: those '100M+ real residential IPs' come from consumer devices, so check sourcing ethics and your target sites' terms before building on it.

video:video.video:title: Thryv Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two published tiers, $85 and $340, and nothing between them. That makes the decision unusually blunt: not which plan fits, but whether a fourfold step is worth taking all at once. And price the commitment from what the page actually says, which is less than you would like: it prints both annual figures per month, states only that the year saves 15%, and never says whether the term is charged up front. Before that call, list which of the bundled parts you would otherwise buy separately: Thryv's case rests on replacing four or five tools, and if you only want two of them the arithmetic usually favours keeping them. Worth knowing too that the Boosts services, the part sold hardest, cannot be attached to Starter at all.

video:video.video:title: TiXel Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The rating is the most useful number on this listing, but not for the reason an average usually is. Read on 18 September 2026 it is 4.6 across 93 reviews, and the shape behind it is 84 five-star, 3 four-star, nothing at three or two, and 6 one-star. A month earlier it was 4.1 across 78, with 7 at the bottom. Nothing sits in the middle on either reading. That is not a mediocre product; it is a binary one: it works immediately, or it installs cleanly and then tracks nothing at all.
The one-star reviews describe the same failure in the same words: the pixel is set up by the instructions, no page views or add-to-carts ever arrive, and support does not reply. We cannot verify what happened in any individual account, but the consistency of the complaint is itself information.
What is new since August is that the developer now answers them in public. A reply dated 2 September 2026 attributes the empty data to manual pixel configuration, where one mismatched ID or event setting is enough to stop events being recorded at all, and says that step is no longer needed: TiXel now integrates officially with Meta and TikTok and links the pixel to your ad account automatically. That is the vendor's account of its own worst reviews, so treat it as a claim to test rather than a fix to trust. It is at least a specific and checkable one, but the trial has shrunk to a single day (it was seven in September), which leaves very little room to check it before you are billed. On 2 November 2026 the record stood at 4.8 across 106 reviews, with 97 five-star and 5 one-star.

video:video.video:title: TicketTailor Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The fee honesty is the product: flat cents per ticket instead of percentage skims makes it dramatically cheaper than the big platforms on higher-priced tickets (a $0.30-0.85 fee on a $50 ticket vs a percentage is no contest). The trade: you bring your own audience. There's no discovery marketplace pushing your event, so if you rely on a platform's browsing traffic to sell out, the cheap fees won't fill seats.

video:video.video:title: Toggl Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Toggl's honesty problem is the good kind: the free tier is so capable that many teams never need to pay: the paid line is drawn exactly at 'do you bill clients' (budgets, rates, profitability). If you do, Starter earns itself fast; if you track time for personal discipline, resist the upgrade. Time tracking's real cost everywhere is adoption: the tool is frictionless, but the habit still has to be built. Two newer cost lines are easy to miss: leave approvals and accruals sit in the $2 Time Off Pro add-on rather than in any plan, and capacity planning beyond the current month is the Capacity Management add-on at $5 to $6 per user, so a team buying Premium for planning should price both.

video:video.video:title: Turbotic Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's a newer, enterprise-leaning automation platform, so it's less proven with a smaller community than the big names, and the credit-per-execution model means heavy volume needs cost-checking. Verify it integrates with your actual stack first.

video:video.video:title: UENI Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's done-for-you, which is the appeal and the catch. DIY editing and customisation are limited, e-commerce and integrations are basic, and the most common complaint is the gap between the 7-day promise and reality: slow design turnaround and patchy communication with the team. Expect some upselling.

video:video.video:title: UltaHost Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's the classic budget-host trade-off, with one thing in its favour. The sticker price is a term commitment: the page opens on the 2-year prices, and the 30/40/50% badges are measured from a crossed-out list price rather than from what monthly billing actually costs, so the real saving for prepaying two years is about 22% on Starter. What works in its favour is the renewal: each card states it renews at the same rate for the same term, so the usual cheap-first-term-then-dear-second trap is at least written down. Read that line on the plan you actually pick. Support is generally fast but can be hit-or-miss depending on which agent picks up your ticket, and it's a smaller, less-established brand than the big managed hosts. It's a value play, not a premium-SLA one.

video:video.video:title: Unleashed Software Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The 100 sales orders a month included on both bundles is the number that decides your bill, not the $399. A wholesaler running 1,500 orders with six users who wants phone support pays $399 for Core, $200 for the order tier, $207 for three extra seats and $99 for Standard support. That is $905 a month, or 2.3 times the headline, before a one-off onboarding fee of at least $449. Support being a paid add-on rather than part of the plan is the detail most comparison tables miss. Price the bundle you will actually be on: count your busiest month's orders, your real seat count, and decide whether you can live without phone support, then compare that total against the alternatives rather than comparing entry prices.

video:video.video:title: Upsell.com Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Growth is banded and cheap up to 500 orders, but the step after Growth is steep. The Shopify listing prints $9.99, $19.99 and $39.99 for the first three paid bands; the 1,000 and 2,000 bands are not in the served page. Past 2,000 orders a month, Scale costs $299 a month ($249 on annual) for a feature set the vendor says is identical on every plan; what it adds is priority chat, guided onboarding and earlier access to features. The pricing page also argues with itself twice: the Scale and Elite cards say billed monthly while the comparison table says annual only, and the annual toggle promises 25% off while the card prices work out at about 17%. Checkout upsells are still Shopify Plus only, so on a standard Shopify plan the checkout stage of the funnel stays shut.

video:video.video:title: UpsellPlus Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The plans are capped by the revenue they are allowed to earn you, and the first paid step does not raise that cap: Free and the $49 Launch plan both stop at $500 of upsell revenue a month. The $49 buys offers and features, not headroom: headroom starts at $119. And crossing a ceiling is not something you decide: their FAQ says you are automatically upgraded to the next tier so the offers keep running, so a good week moves the invoice on its own. Read the feature list closely too, because the tier named Shopify Plus is not the same thing as the requirement: their FAQ says Plus is needed only for checkout customization and checkout upsells, so on a standard Shopify store the checkout half of a checkout-upsell app is not what you are buying. The last thing to know is at the top, and it is not on their pricing page. The plan card says Scale stops at $5,000 a month while the comparison table on that same page says Unlimited; we asked, and UpsellPlus support confirmed on 21 September 2026 that Scale is a revenue ladder - $199 up to $5,000 of upsell revenue a month, $299 up to $10,000, $399 up to $15,000, $499 up to $20,000, $699 up to $30,000, $799 up to $40,000, and an Unlimited plan at $999 with no ceiling - and that passing $5,000 moves a store to the $299 tier on its own. That is better news than the Enterprise tier above it suggests, but it means the number you are quoted at signup is the floor of a ladder whose higher rungs are not published anywhere.

video:video.video:title: UptimeRobot Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The famous free tier is real, but the paid ladder has quiet extras: extra login seats cost $15-19 per month EACH beyond the included ones, and SMS or voice-call alerts are pay-per-credit on every plan. The Solo tier includes no team seats at all.

video:video.video:title: VEA Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The pitch is unusually bold: an AI that learns your business the way a great employee would, finds the constraint keeping you stuck, and helps you solve it. That ambition is also the honest caveat: it's a young product making a big promise, its price ladder was rebuilt in August 2026 with a top tier at $597 per user a month, and independent review coverage is still thin (one rating on the US App Store on 29 September 2026). Judge it in the 7-day trial on one measurable question: did it identify a constraint you recognize as painfully real? If yes, it earns the next month. If its advice stays generic, the thing its own positioning promises to avoid, walk.

video:video.video:title: Velora Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Velora is three acquired products (Keela, Aplos, Raisely) being unified into one platform, and that's the honest watch-out: integration between them is newer than the marketing suggests, so check how deeply the pieces actually connect for your workflow before committing. Costs also stack per product and per contact count: a growing donor base raises the CRM bill. For nonprofits though, purpose-built beats adapted business software in fund accounting specifically.

video:video.video:title: VidPal Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Credits don't carry over month to month, and a few users report slow support/account responses, so run the free plan through a full create-and-publish loop before you pay.

video:video.video:title: Vista Social Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It undercuts the big suites convincingly. The honest check is coverage depth: platform APIs change constantly, so verify the specific networks and features YOUR clients need (particularly newer TikTok/threads capabilities and approval workflows) inside the trial rather than trusting the comparison table. Agencies stepping up from Professional hit the Scale tier for white-labeling: price that step into client contracts from day one.

video:video.video:title: Warmup Inbox Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The pricing is published and readable: three tiers, per inbox, with both billing toggles printing a rate: $19, $59 and $99 monthly, or $15, $49 and $79 on the yearly plan. The bigger caveat is structural: warmup is priced per inbox, so a team running twenty sending addresses pays for twenty, although the published volume ladder brings Pro down to $35 an inbox on yearly billing from fifteen inboxes. And warmup is a floor, not a ceiling: it builds sender reputation, but no amount of it rescues a bad list or a bad offer.

video:video.video:title: Way Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The pricing page reads like a feature ladder and behaves like a counter. Basic, Advanced and Pro list the same eight capabilities, so the $8 and $23 steps above Basic buy nothing but a higher location limit, and the jump from 50 to 500 leaves no tier in between. A chain with 60 or 80 shops pays the 500-location price and uses a tenth of it.
The free plan is usable on a live store, which is worth saying plainly: the same developer's Blocky and TiXel listings advertise free plans that turn out to be development stores only, and this one is not that. What it does carry is the app's branding on your storefront and a hard limit of one location, so it is a real free tier for a single shop rather than a trial in disguise.

video:video.video:title: WebCatalog Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It solves a real annoyance: dozens of web apps and multiple accounts per app as tidy desktop windows. The honest question is whether you need the paid tier at all. The free plan's 2-app limit is tight, but browser profiles and PWAs solve part of the same problem for free. Pro earns its fee when multi-account juggling (several Gmail/Slack/WhatsApp identities) is daily reality. Three practical limits come from WebCatalog's own documentation, read 21 October 2026: DRM-protected video does not play in the desktop app, Linux support is experimental without a promise of distribution-specific help, and because login sessions never leave the device, a new laptop means signing in to every app again even though the app list syncs.

video:video.video:title: Webflow Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Three separate bills, and the pricing page shows them on separate tabs. A site plan is what puts your site online: $15 a month for a static site, $25 with the CMS. A workspace plan is what lets your team work on it: $19 or $49 a month. And seats are charged on top of the workspace plan at $39 a month each for anyone who can actually design. So a two-person team on a CMS site is not $25 a month: it is $25 for the site, $19 for the workspace and $39 for the second seat, which is $83, and that is before add-ons. Two more numbers to find before you commit. The entry ecommerce plan takes a 2% transaction fee on every order, which the $29 headline does not mention and which is the largest single cost for anyone selling real volume; removing it means Plus at $74. And Optimize, the conversion tooling Webflow leads with in its marketing, starts at $299 a month on top of everything else and is priced by page views. Price your team, your site and your add-ons together, because no single tab on that page shows you a total.

video:video.video:title: Weblium Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Starter caps a site at 10 pages and 5 GB of bandwidth and has no blog or online store; those need Business. Every subscription covers one website, and moving to a cheaper plan only works after the current term ends. The Free plan is limited to 3 pages, 100 MB storage and 100 MB bandwidth, and a Free site goes offline 46 days after its 14-day trial and is deleted 60 days after that. During the trial a site cannot be indexed, connect a domain or show form replies in readable form. Weblium's own savings figures disagree: the pricing page claims up to 67% off for paying yearly, its FAQ and the September 2026 pricing post say up to 30%, and the bundle help article from 2024 says up to 50% against 25-40% on the pricing page.

video:video.video:title: Wegic Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Everything is credits, and generating a site burns them fast: Wegic's own page notes a single generation can cost over $10 in credits, while the free plan gives 100 credits once. The cheaper per-credit rate only kicks in on the higher annual tier, and premium AI media draws down a second 'Cloud' balance on top of your plan.

video:video.video:title: WhatConverts Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The meter is honest and only half of it is printed: every phone number, call minute, text, form, chat, appointment, email, event and transaction is charged against a monthly credit. The comparison table on the pricing page prints the phone rates past that credit: $2.50 a local number, 4.5 cents a local minute, 3 cents a text on the single-account plans, but for forms, chats and transactions it prints only the included allowance (up to 300 on Plus, Pro and Elite) and no rate beyond it. You can still model the bill: the calculator on the pricing page turns a monthly volume into a usage figure, and on 10 September 2026 it put the $30 Call Tracking plan at no extra usage for 50 calls and 100 forms, $47 at 500 of each and $250 at 2,000 of each. Its genuine strength versus bigger attribution suites is capturing EVERY lead type (not just calls) at a fair price; the flip side is you still need someone to read the reports and reallocate budget, or it's measurement theater.

video:video.video:title: WhisperTranscribe Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Starter's card advertises $2.80 an hour, but 320 minutes for $19.99 a month is about $3.75 an hour, our arithmetic. Monthly billing costs twice the annual rate on every plan, and fees and unused credits are non-refundable under the terms. Transcripts are not kept on the vendor's servers after delivery, which is good for privacy but means a lost local copy is gone. Some AI processing runs in the United States. The pricing page says translation into 99 languages while its comparison table says 65+. The terms of 20 October 2026 add a 14-day withdrawal right for EU, EEA and UK consumers on subscriptions, refunded minus the service already used; buying a credit package gives up that right once the credits are in your account. Subscription minutes expire every cycle, and the terms cap liability at the fees paid in the previous 12 months, or €0 for a user who paid nothing.

video:video.video:title: Wholesale Gorilla Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It is a feature ladder, not a volume ladder, and the features most people picture when they say wholesale sit high on it. Volume discounts (buy ten, pay less each) are Premium only, at $149.95 a month, more than four times the entry price. Discount codes, net payment terms, wholesale shipping rules and theme integration all start at Advanced, $69.95. Lite at $34.95 buys custom prices per customer group and a basic signup form, which is a price list rather than a wholesale channel. Work out which rung you actually need before you read $34.95 as your price, because the honest entry point for most wholesale operations is the middle one.

video:video.video:title: Wing Assistant Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: You're renting a person, not automating a task: a good VA is real leverage, but only if you already have documented, delegatable work. Hand over chaos and you'll get chaos back, faster.

video:video.video:title: Wistia Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Bandwidth is the meter that decides your bill, and it is the one number you cannot predict before you publish. A single video that does well can move you from Free to Business in a month, which is arguably the product working, but budget for it rather than being surprised. Their FAQ, as read on 19 September 2026, was precise about which way it cuts: free accounts cannot exceed their bandwidth limit, while paid plans are billed for usage beyond what is included or prepaid. The free tier carries Wistia branding on the player, so it is a trial with no time limit rather than a plan you can ship a brand on. The published prices are the annual ones; the page's toggle sits on Annual with a 20% saving and the month-to-month figures are not in its source, so a monthly subscriber cannot price the plan from the pricing page. The webinar overages were the sharpest edge on that reading: $2.00 per extra minute means a session that runs long costs real money, the allowance is per event rather than cumulative, and the shortened FAQ of 19 October 2026 no longer prints either figure, so confirm them before you book a long session.

video:video.video:title: Wiz Checkout Upsell Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The name says checkout, but the $49 Essential plan does not include checkout upsells. That tier is post-purchase, thank-you page and order status page only, and the listing explicitly marks it as not applicable for Shopify Plus. Everything the app is named after: checkout upsells, checkout banners and trust badges, input fields, gift messages, free gifts at checkout: starts on the $99 Plus Growth plan. There is no free plan either, only a 14-day trial; as of 19 September that tier carries a BFCM offer of $1 for the first month, undated, so today the cheapest honest look at checkout upsells is a dollar and after this promotion it is $99 a month again. And A/B testing across all extensions, the feature you would want precisely to prove that $99 was worth it, sits one rung higher again at $199, even though the listing advertises built-in A/B testing in its own highlights.

video:video.video:title: Woodpecker Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The $7-per-100-prospects unit reads cheap, but a real outbound motion stacks add-ons fast. Every connected LinkedIn account is $29 a month, managed sending addresses $6 a month apiece and extra warm-ups $5 per account, and contacted prospects are the meter, so scaling outreach scales the bill.

video:video.video:title: Wrike Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's powerful and scales to complex, cross-team portfolios, but that power brings a learning curve and a per-seat cost that climbs: small teams often find it heavier than they need next to a simpler board tool.

video:video.video:title: Xero Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Read the second number, not the first. Every plan on the US page is 80% off for three months, and the price after that is five times what the button says: $27, $59 and $97 a month. Those standard rates rose on 1 October 2026 from $25, $55 and $90. The second thing to check is the entry tier's ceiling: Early is 20 invoices and 5 bills a month, auto-reconcile costs $5 a month extra on it, and on our September reading the invoice limit counted approving as well as sending, with connected apps able to use it up. That makes Growing at $59 the realistic starting price for anyone billing through other software. And check which country's page you are on, because Xero's tiers and prices differ by market.

video:video.video:title: Zedonk Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The 'starting from' wording is doing real work: £166/mo is the floor of the cheapest module, billed annually, so a working setup for a brand that sells wholesale quickly stacks toward £332/mo and beyond: about £4,000 a year before add-ons. There is no trial and no public total: you find out your actual price in a demo call. Budget for the stack, not the sticker.

video:video.video:title: Zeffy Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest scrutiny of 'free': the tip prompt is shown to YOUR donors, with suggested percentages. Most give happily, but some organizations feel it inserts a step between donor and cause, and a donor who tips 10% effectively paid a fee, just voluntarily and not from your share. Compare that trade against the 2-5% the paid platforms take from every donation, and for most small nonprofits the math strongly favors Zeffy.

video:video.video:title: ZenBusiness Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The $0 is real for the filing service and it is also the whole commercial idea: what you sign up for at zero has an annual carry that is not shown next to it. A registered agent is a legal requirement in every state, and theirs is $199/year, so the realistic first-year cost of 'the $0 LLC' is the state fee plus $199, before compliance filing at another $199/year. Price the second year, not the first. The second thing to hold in view is that the state fee is the largest and most variable number in the whole exercise, and ZenBusiness cannot change it. It is set by your state, ranges widely, and their own page sends you to a lookup rather than quoting it. Anyone comparing formation services on the advertised price alone is comparing the small half of the bill.

video:video.video:title: Zendrop Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The free plan is a catalogue browser rather than a working tier: it allows no linked products, so nothing can actually be sold through it. Past that you are paying for an allowance, not for capability: Beginner, Pro and Plus carry exactly the same feature list, and the only thing $79 buys over $29 is room for more than a hundred linked products. The subscription is also the smaller half of the bill: product and shipping cost lands per order on top, and Zendrop bills that separately from your Shopify invoice, so the figure you budget is not the figure you pay. Their own pricing page and the App Store listing do not agree: the site sells Free, Pro and Plus with annual rates and no $29 tier, which means the price depends on where you sign up. And the 4.5 average covers a split verdict, with 83% five stars alongside 7% one star across 1,264 reviews (read 5 October 2026): 86 people rating it bottom of the scale.

video:video.video:title: Zoviz Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
Zoviz lets you design for free and charges when you download, and downloading also ends your refund: the FAQ allows a refund within 30 days only if no files were downloaded and no AI credits used. There is no one-off logo price on the pricing page; the FAQ's own advice for a logo is a month's subscription, €29 on Starter. The AI credits that drive the marketing tools are not priced per task on the page, expire every billing cycle and are topped up with separately sold packs. Prices change with your location: euros from the Netherlands, a $399 first-year figure for Pro in the page's own US-dollar table. The '4.9/5 from 12,000+ reviews' claim names no source. We have not used Zoviz ourselves.
Zoviz's own pages give two refund rules. The pricing FAQ allows a request within 30 days of purchase if nothing was downloaded and no AI credits were used; the help centre's billing page says that if nothing was used there is no time limit. Both agree that downloading a file counts as use. Ask from your account email with the invoice ID, as the help centre instructs.
Cancelling costs more than the plan. When access ends, unused plan credits are forfeited, published Link in Bio pages and digital business cards go offline, the brands your plan unlocked lock again, and designs saved in the cloud lock; the cancel screen says they are deleted after 90 days. Files you downloaded while subscribed keep their commercial-use rights. A failed renewal ends the plan straight away, with the same effects, and a new card can take up to 2 business days to go through.
Starter includes the website builder, but the help centre says publishing a website needs Pro or Business. The terms place disputes under US law, with the courts and arbitration centre of New York.

video:video.video:title: iContact Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Pricing feels a touch high for what you get, and the Standard plan's hard caps on automations and landing pages push growing teams to upgrade sooner than expected. Set against ActiveCampaign the automation builder is the thinner half of the deal; what iContact sells instead is a product you can hold in your head, deliverability that holds up, and a human on support included rather than sold as a tier.

video:video.video:title: iubenda Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Prices are per site, and each plan has a pageview quota (25K, 50K or 150K a month) with €0.05 per 1,000 above it. Essentials allows one language and up to 20 policy clauses; multilingual sites start on Advanced at €19.99 a month. The free plan's limits are not on the pricing page. We have not used iubenda ourselves. iubenda's own documents disagree on tax: the pricing page says prices exclude VAT, while the pricing FAQs say prices include VAT where applicable; the same FAQs give a 14-day money-back guarantee on purchases and renewals. If you stop paying, a paid privacy policy cannot stay in use, though a policy generated on Free stays free, and a downgrade to Essentials switches off the terms and conditions document, which only Advanced and Ultimate include.

video:video.video:title: monday.com Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The seat price is not the product price. monday sells four products (Work Management, CRM, Dev and Service) each on its own subscription, and the $9 you see first is the cheapest tier of one of them. A sales team that wants the CRM is buying a second subscription on top of whatever Work Management costs, with a three-seat minimum of its own. The second number to find before you commit is the automation cap. Standard allows 250 automation actions a month across the whole account. If you are buying monday because of the automations you saw demoed, 250 is roughly one workflow running a few times a day, and the next step up is Pro at $19 a seat against Standard's $12. Free is capped at two seats and three boards, which makes it a preview rather than a plan. On payment, the FAQ excludes debit cards (credit card or PayPal, depending on location) and accepts invoices only for Enterprise orders above a minimum fee it does not state, which can rule monday out for a small company that pays by bank transfer.
